cia-0000015265: Flying objects were seen in the Saransk area, in a CIA report dated October 1, 1955. Saransk lay in the middle Volga lands of the Soviet Union. Reports from deep inside the USSR were prized and doubted at once. The file keeps one such claim from a town few Americans could have named.
cia-0000015365: Current status of the Unidentified Flying Objects project fills a CIA file dated November 4, 1953. The project is named UFOB in the title's code. A status note means the work had bosses who wanted progress in writing. By late 1953 the project was sorting sightings in a steady, clerks' rhythm. The UFOB status report is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015465: Spain and North Africa produced flying saucer reports in a CIA record dated July 3, 1952. That summer ranks among the busiest of the whole saucer era in America and Europe. Southern reports widened the map well past the Atlantic world. The agency gathered them country by country, building a world picture of a wave that no single office could explain away.
cia-0000022365: Belgrade's Serbian radio carried the Powers trial, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. Yugoslavia stood outside both blocs, so its airwaves reached listeners East and West. Carrying the Moscow trial gave Belgrade a neutral stage in a superpower quarrel. The entry shows the trial's audience stretching well past the courtroom and the two rival capitals.
cia-0000036565:
A CIA report dated March 3, 1969 covers Daniel R. Nidds under the Bright Light project. Bright Light was the effort to find and account for Americans missing or held prisoner in Southeast Asia. The report is one case file inside that much larger search.

Inside, the focus stays on one man: what was known about Nidds and what remained unclear. Case files like this were built piece by piece from sightings, lists, and witness accounts. They show the slow, careful work behind the public promise that no one would be forgotten. Nidds is named in the title itself, which keeps the file personal rather than general.
cia-0000037165:
American prisoners of war were reported held in Savannakhet province in Laos, in a CIA record dated October 1, 1981. Savannakhet lies in southern Laos, along the Mekong River. Laos held some of the least settled cases in the whole accounting. Many of its missing men were airmen lost over jungle and mountain country.

The record preserves the report of prisoners held in that one province. Laotian cases were hard because the wartime records there were thin and access was rare. The file shows the search reaching into the Mekong country in 1981. It still followed reports about men lost in a war that Laos had never openly admitted fighting.
cia-0000045165:
A Zona Rosa detainee described the PRTC organization, in a CIA record dated July 6, 1985. The detainee had been held over the attack in the Zona Rosa district. Prisoners' accounts can open a closed group to outside view.

Inside, the detainee's picture of the faction is set down. Structure, names, and habits are what such debriefs are made of. Analysts prize them because factions hide exactly those facts. The file preserves one inside view of the PRTC in 1985. It came from a man in custody. His words had to be weighed with care by every reader of the report.
cia-0000049065: An armed forces officer in El Salvador was detained in 1983 for a human rights violation, on orders from above, and a CIA item records the detention. Arrests of officers for abuses were rare enough to be news inside the files. The item survives in the Truth Commission records as one early sign of discipline attempted.
cia-0000049265: Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney put a question in 1990 about political killings in El Salvador, and a CIA item preserves it. When the Pentagon's chief asked, the question itself was policy: the military's patience with its Salvadoran partners was being measured. The item survives among the Truth Commission records of those years.
cia-0000049365: Security Situation in Central America is the title of declassified CIA document 0000049365, dated September 3, 1983. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper surveys security conditions across the region. The brief file preserves the agency's chosen subject in its heading. It offers a dated snapshot topic. It comes from a period when Central America filled much of the agency's reporting.
cia-0000075265: Situation and Prospects in Brazil is the title of declassified CIA document 0000075265, dated June 3, 1963. The paper pairs a present situation with an outlook, in standard estimate style. Readers find a short declassified country item whose heading gives its double purpose, preserved as one of the agency's Brazil records from the early nineteen sixties.
cia-0000094965: Third Report to the President by the President's Board of Consultants on Foreign Intelligence Activities, in the catalog's shortened wording, is declassified CIA document 0000094965, dated September 6, 1959. The file is a report from a presidential advisory board. Readers get a dated board report record, one of several such reports preserved in the declassified collection.
cia-0000097665: The Crisis in China is the title of declassified CIA document 0000097665, dated June 5, 1966. Four words carry the whole heading, crisis named without detail. Readers find a short declassified paper under that stark title, one of the agency's many China items. It is distinguished by the bluntness of its subject line. Its scope, by contrast, stays unstated.
cia-0000098265: Some Perspectives on the Dominican Problem is the title of declassified CIA document 0000098265, dated September 3, 1965. The heading offers perspectives, plural, on a problem it does not define further. The brief file is a declassified viewpoints paper on the Dominican question, a softer companion to the formal stability estimate filed the next year.
cia-0000102965:
The Soviet Forced Labor System: An Update is declassified CIA document 0000102965, dated November 1, 1985, with that date marked as an estimate. Its opening calls the Gulag still a Soviet reality. It argues forced labor was part of the economy and a tool for keeping citizens in line.

The update puts forced laborers at over four and a half million, about three percent of the total Soviet labor force. About two million were confined in roughly twelve hundred camps, with more in urban prisons and colony settlements. Unconfined laborers, including parolees and probationers sent to labor projects, added about two and a quarter million more.
cia-0000106265: Expansion Into the DRV-Lao Border - Resistance Effort is the subject of an untitled declassified CIA document 0000106265, dated June 3, 1965. The catalog marks the file untitled, then gives this subject line on border resistance. DRV names North Vietnam, and Lao names Laos, in the heading's short forms. The brief record is a border item from the Vietnam War years.
cia-0000109065: Dated November 5, 1968, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000109065 records a Cuban official's views on future Cuban-United States relations. Its heading breaks off at Cuban-united St, mid-phrase in the title. The official is not named in the heading itself at all. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000119765: An October 1956 CIA report collects reactions to the Polish and Hungarian developments of that month. Two communist states had defied Moscow at once, and capitals from Washington to Beijing were recalculating. The paper gathers the responses as they reached the agency. Collecting foreign reaction was standard crisis work, since each government's stance hinted at votes, statements, and pressure that might follow at the United Nations.
cia-0000124265: A July 1959 CIA report, numbered PD 3-68, covers Soviet research and development in very low frequency radio work. Such waves can reach submarines far below the surface, a link both fleets prized during the Cold War. The report follows Moscow's work on that hidden channel. Very low frequency waves bend around the earth and pierce seawater to a shallow depth, which is why navies guarded this corner of the spectrum closely.
cia-0000126865: An April 1965 CIA report bears the heading Tanzania Taking the Left Turn. Under Nyerere, the young country was moving toward an African form of socialism that worried Washington. The paper tracks that leftward course two years before the Arusha Declaration set it in words. Left-turn reports watched trade, aid, and party language for signs of direction, treating a young state's socialism as a question of alignment as much as economics.
cia-0000126965: Dated November 1965, this CIA report covers a revolt by hard-line dissidents inside the FALN against its established leadership, the heading breaking off. Venezuela's guerrilla movement was tearing itself apart from within. The paper tracks that internal rebellion as reported to the agency. Guerrilla splits were good news in the analysts' ledger, since a movement fighting itself spent strength that might otherwise have gone against the government it opposed.
cia-0000132165: Situation report 482 in the January 1991 Iraq-Kuwait series gathers further reactions to an Iraqi missile attack, the heading breaking off. Missile strikes on Israel and Saudi Arabia were reshaping the war's politics. The report collects those responses as they arrived. Reaction gathering after each missile strike served a single question: would Israel strike back and widen the war, or hold and keep the coalition together.
cia-0000132265: Situation report 572, dated January 1991, judges Saddam's ceasefire bid as less than it seems, the heading breaking off mid-phrase. Such bids served as weapons in the diplomatic contest of that winter. The report takes the offer apart for the watch. Ceasefire bids in the final weeks were read in Washington as tests of the deadline's firmness, and this sitrep's blunt verdict shows the reading given that day.
cia-0000132565:
Under the running title Cuban Developments, this CIA briefing of October 4, 1960 tracks the revolution's progress into the fall. The series kept officials supplied with regular updates on Castro's Cuba. By that autumn, the United States was planning Castro's removal.

Series papers like this one valued continuity: each entry measured what had changed since the last. The October entry belongs to the months when exile plans were hardening and relations had nearly collapsed. Declassified long afterward, it offers one dated snapshot inside a year-long surveillance rhythm, preserved through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000132665: A communist from El Salvador reportedly seeking Cuban backing fills a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. The small Salvadoran left saw Cuba as both a model and a patron. Leftists across the region were turning to Havana for money, training, and hope that year. The short paper reports the approach and what the man was said to want.
cia-0000132765: A third CIA briefing on Cuba dated May 4, 1960 shows how much paper the island generated in a single day. Spring 1960 was a turning point in relations, and the volume of reporting proves Washington's focus. This entry adds one more angle to that day's file. The declassified text comes from the CIA Reading Room via the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134265: Guerrilla action that would not quit, and its effect on Castro, fill item 12 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated March 2, 1960. Its headline misspells persistence as perisitence, a slip kept from the original. The guerrillas in question were anti-Castro rebels fighting in the Escambray hills. The short item reports their staying power.
cia-0000136265: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 1 May 1954, covers Instruction 13 for broadcasts, the radio war's script book grown long by the first of May. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136565: A document in Spanish dated 4 November 1960, from the declassified files of Brigade 2506, the CIA's Cuban exile force. November 1960 was a busy month in the brigade's surviving record. The catalog title for this item names no subject. Preserved in Spanish, it is a dated fragment of the paperwork generated while the brigade trained for a landing its members believed would topple Castro. The record is presented as the agency released it.
cia-0000136765: This Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade files is dated, by estimate, to 1 January 1961; the catalog flags the date as estimated. The brigade of anti-Castro exiles was in its final training winter. No subject appears in the record for the item. Preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, it is one of the turn-of-the-year brigade records whose timing is approximate.
cia-0000136865: Ways to reach the field are listed in this March 1954 cable to LINCOLN. One route runs through commercial channels. Another is an active agency radio station. That station keeps daily schedules at set hours. A third station shares a schedule with it. A signal plan allows contact at any time of day. One remote station is a weak link. Its messages arrive late or not at all. Until a new radio is installed, other channels must carry the load.
cia-0000136965: A New York radio newscast from 1716 on 20 June 1954 is excerpted in this cable, and its theme is Guatemala's forum shopping. Delegates of Brazil, Mexico, and another country requested hearings in the OAS rather than the UN, the broadcast says. Guatemala wants a UN hearing, the commentary runs, due to the Soviet and other communist votes there, depicting foreigners as having invaded and hoping the UN's usual Soviet line would help. The fragment preserves how headquarters monitored American airwaves during the invasion week.
cia-0000137465: Kennedy's trip was a great success, Director John McCone writes in January 1962. The December 1961 visit covered Venezuela and Colombia. It may mark a turning point in relations with Latin America. The memo sums up agency work supporting the visit. Current intelligence still warns of active opposition. In Venezuela, leftists opposing Betancourt stay active. Sabotage incidents against American property are reported. In Colombia, the government faces serious rural unrest and violence. The memo was released through the JFK Library review.
cia-0000141165:
Colonel Stanley W. Beerli of the Air Force signed a CIA memo on 26 April 1961, nine days after the Bay of Pigs landing in Cuba. Sent to Colonel B. W. Tarwater at the Joint Chiefs, it forwards a full packet on the air war. The packet holds a short narrative of air action and a timeline of events, both filed under one case number.

More parts follow: a report from the base called Tide on planes, crews, targets, and takeoff times, plus notes on pilot training. One part lists support drop flights from D-Day through D+2. Others name the staff who trained the pilots and give the makeup of the base unit at Tide.
cia-06156965: 1. POISON GAS ATTACKS ON HMONG TRIBE MEMBERS 2. "BLACK RAIN" LETHAL CW AGENT, a CIA document. The Laos allegations. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
cia-06943665: HR- FITNESS REPORT - ELIZABETH SUDMEIER, a CIA document. The personnel file. This file preserves that declassified paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
comte-positivism-bridges-1865:
Auguste Comte published A General View of Positivism in French in 1848. The English text here is J. H. Bridges's translation of 1865. Comte sums up his system for general readers. Positivism, he argues, can reorganize society after revolution's chaos. Science gives the method, and the religion of humanity gives the bond.

He outlines a positivist polity with priests of humanity, festivals, and a new calendar of secular saints. Many readers admired the science and balked at the religion. Bridges led the English positivist movement that spread Comte's ideas. The book is Comte's own shortest summary of his thought. It shows both his power and his strangeness.
europmc-pmc10060165:
Zhang and a large team present faster, more sensitive GCaMP calcium indicators for filming nerve cell activity, in a 2023 study. GCaMP sensors glow when calcium rises inside a cell, which lets scientists watch neurons fire in a living brain. Older sensors were too slow to track rapid firing and forced a trade-off between speed and brightness.

The new sensors aim to break that trade-off. The team tested them in cells and in animal brains. Their results show sharper tracking of fast neural signals. The tools should help labs map how large groups of neurons work together.
europmc-pmc10232365:
Schultz and co-authors report that ancient gene linkages support comb jellies as the sister group to all other animals, in a 2023 study. Which came first, sponges or comb jellies, is a deep puzzle in animal evolution. The answer changes how scientists think the first nervous systems and muscles arose.

The team compared the arrangement of genes on chromosomes across animals. Those arrangements change very slowly, so they hold ancient signals. The patterns point to comb jellies as the earliest branch. The study offers a fresh line of evidence in a long debate.
europmc-pmc10287165:
Carlini and co-authors review interleukin-10, a versatile immune signal, in a 2023 paper. IL-10 mainly calms inflammation and protects the body from its own overactive defenses. It acts through a known signaling chain in many cell types, and its effects reach far beyond a simple off switch.

The review covers how IL-10 is regulated and what it does in steady health. It then follows its roles in cancer, COVID-19, and the long symptoms that can follow COVID. The authors weigh its promise as both a drug and a drug target.
europmc-pmc10394065:
Yang and co-authors reviewed support cells in tumours in 2023 and how to target them. The cells are cancer-associated fibroblasts, the main builders of the tissue around a tumour. They trade signals with cancer cells and shape how a tumour grows and spreads. Cancer cells can train them, and the cells can shift form with ease.

That ease makes the group hard to pin down. Yang sums up where these cells may come from and how subtypes differ. The review also covers gene switches that drive each subtype. Some subtypes help the tumour, while others may restrain it. Care plans must hit the harmful kinds and spare the rest, Yang argues.
europmc-pmc10589265:
Sun and a large team found in 2023 a copper-driven cell death path that may be turned on stomach cancer. The death, cuproptosis, strikes when copper builds up too high in a cell. Copper levels run high in gastric tumours, most of all in the worst ones. The team hunted for the genes that let this death proceed.

A gene editor called METTL16 stood out as a key driver. Sun shows it tags the message of a second gene, FDX1, which the death path needs. Copper stress adds a lactate tag to METTL16 that boosts its act. A drug that ferries copper, elesclomol, killed tumours better when that tag rose. Pairing it with a blocker of the tag-remover SIRT2 worked in mice.
europmc-pmc1069665:
Haubner and co-authors tested a scan tracer in 2005 to see a tumour marker in patients with no surgery. The marker, integrin alpha-v beta-3, helps tumours grow new blood vessels and spread. A labelled sugar compound, Galacto-RGD, binds that marker. PET scans can then show where it sits in the body.

In mice, tracer uptake in tumours matched marker levels read later in the lab. Haubner shows the scan could flag marker that came from tumour vessels alone. In patients with cancer, the scans gave a clear, counted map of the marker on tumour and vessel cells. Such maps may help plan and track drugs that block vessel growth.
europmc-pmc1240665:
McGeehin and Mirabelli assessed heat risks under climate change in 2001. Heat waves are expected to grow stronger and more frequent. City studies tie sharp heat rises to more deaths. Harm peaks when heat tops what locals are used to.

Models suggest Northeast and Midwest cities face the largest burden. City dwellers are most at risk overall. The elderly, young children, and the poor face extra danger. So do people who are bedridden or on certain drugs. McGeehin notes most heat illness can be prevented. Cooling, behavior change, and planning save lives.
europmc-pmc1257465:
Stogios and co-authors analyzed BTB domain proteins across 17 species in 2005. The BTB domain is a protein segment that links proteins together. It serves jobs from gene control to channel assembly. Some BTB proteins feed targets to cell disposal machinery.

Sequences and structures were compared across 17 fully sequenced eukaryotes. The domain shape proved highly conserved through evolution. Proteins varied in how they pair with themselves and partners. That variety lets one scaffold serve many cell tasks. Stogios maps where BTB proteins occur across genomes. Their pairing modes explain much of the family range.
europmc-pmc1277865:
Künzli and colleagues linked air pollution to artery thickening in Los Angeles in 2005. Long-term pollution exposure ties to heart disease and death. Whether pollution feeds atherosclerosis, the artery plaque process, was untested in people. Data came from 798 adults in two clinical trials.

Neck artery wall thickness measured silent atherosclerosis. Home addresses gave yearly fine particle exposure estimates. Exposure ranged from 5.2 to 26.9 micrograms per cubic meter. Each 10-unit exposure contrast tied to 5.9 percent thicker walls. Age adjustment shrank but did not erase the link. Künzli gives human evidence pollution may build plaque.
europmc-pmc1557665:
Where children live may shape how active they are. Davison and Lawson reviewed 33 studies in 2006 on the built surroundings and kids' activity, for ages 3 to 18. They sorted findings into play facilities, transport setup, and local conditions.

Access to parks, recreation sites, and schools went with more activity. So did sidewalks, safe crossings, and public transport. Heavy traffic and many roads to cross went with less activity. Crime and area deprivation also held children back. Davison calls for studies that test how these factors mix, so policy can target what truly moves children.
europmc-pmc1564165:
Life expectancy in the United States splits sharply by race and place. Murray and co-authors divided the nation into eight Americas in 2006, grouping people by race, county, income, and homicide rates. The gap between the best and worst groups topped 35 years.

Asian women, the longest lived, outlived high-risk urban black men by 20.7 years. Gaps were widest in young and middle-aged adults. Chronic diseases and injuries with known risk factors drove most of the divide. From 1982 to 2001, the ranking and the size of the gap barely moved. Murray argues policy must target each America's distinct risks.
europmc-pmc1779365:
Gertz, Schäffer, Altschul and their co-authors described in 2006 how a key search tool for genes was improved. The tool is TBLASTN, part of the BLAST package used to match proteins to DNA. TBLASTN reads DNA in all six possible frames, meaning the three reading starts on each strand.

The paper gives the first full account of the modern form of TBLASTN. Its new method, called composition-based statistics, uses the makeup of the sequences being matched to set fairer E-values. An E-value estimates how likely a match is by chance. Tests used 1,000 searches with scrambled mouse proteins against human chromosomes, plus a rebuilt test set for finding known matches. The new scoring made the stated accuracy far more true, at a small cost in finding matches.
europmc-pmc1779465:
Ma and colleagues pooled earlier studies in 2006 to ask whether childbearing history affects breast cancer types in distinct ways. Breast tumors differ by whether they carry receptors, which are docking sites for the hormones estrogen and progesterone. The team studied births, the age when a woman first gives birth, breastfeeding, and age at first period.

This was the first such pooling split by joint receptor status. Each birth cut the risk of receptor-positive cancer by 11 percent, and the oldest group at first birth faced 27 percent higher risk than the youngest group. Neither factor changed risk for receptor-negative cancer. Breastfeeding and a later first period lowered risk for both tumor types. The authors suggest the factors act through distinct hormone paths.
europmc-pmc1790865:
Blanvillain, Arlat and colleagues showed in 2007 that some plant-attacking bacteria scavenge plant sugars through gates long known only for iron uptake. The gates are TonB-dependent receptors, proteins in the outer membrane of certain bacteria. The plant pathogen Xanthomonas campestris carries 72 of them, far more than most bacteria.

One receptor proved to carry sucrose, common plant sugar, with very high affinity, meaning it grabs the sugar tightly. It works with an inner transporter, an enzyme, and a regulator as a named unit, the CUT locus. Losing that locus weakened the bacterium's attack on Arabidopsis plants. Related loci target other plant carbohydrates, and similar gate-rich systems occur in water bacteria that break down complex carbohydrates.
europmc-pmc1794565:
Lee, Ausubel and co-authors sequenced in 2006 a highly virulent strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common soil bacterium that infects burns and weakened patients. They compared its genome with a previously sequenced, less harmful strain. The aim was to learn which gene sets make this species dangerous.

The comparison showed no single master virulence factor. Instead, harm came from combinations of genes, many gathered in pathogenicity islands, which are clusters of disease genes often gained from other bacteria. The team tested candidate genes in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, a standard lab host for infection studies. Mutants lacking single genes often stayed virulent, while the strain's overall makeup set its strength. Their verdict is in the title's claim: virulence here is combinatorial, built from many parts acting together.
europmc-pmc1865565:
Slagter, Davidson and co-authors tested in 2007 whether intensive meditation frees up brain attention resources. In the attentional blink task, a second target flashed soon after a first is often missed. The miss is blamed on the two targets competing for limited processing resources.

Volunteers took the task before and after three months of intensive mental training. After training, the blink shrank: the second target was seen more often. Brain recordings showed a smaller P3b wave to the first target, a signal that indexes how many resources a stimulus grabs. Spending fewer resources on the first target left more for the second. People whose first-target signal shrank most gained most on the blink measure. The results show training can sharpen control over scarce attention.
europmc-pmc1904465:
Killeen and colleagues modeled in 2007 how widely insecticide-treated bed nets must be used to stop malaria in Africa. Nets are a practical shield, and global goals aimed to cover 80 percent of pregnant women and young children by 2010. That targeting logic ignores protection that spills over to the whole community when mosquito numbers fall.

Using transmission models fitted to field data, they compared targeted-only coverage with population-wide coverage. Giving nets to 80 percent of the vulnerable groups, who form under 20 percent of people, delivered limited and unequal protection. In contrast, 35 to 65 percent use across all adults and children matched that protection level, with the threshold set by local ecology and net quality. Broad modest coverage can thus beat narrow intense coverage, a finding with direct policy weight.
europmc-pmc2065865:
Farivar, Cunningham and Hays proposed a new scoring method in 2007 for two widely used health surveys, the SF-36 and SF-12. These questionnaires summarise physical and mental health in two scores. Standard scoring forces those two scores to be unrelated, called an orthogonal solution. The team instead allowed the scores to correlate, reflecting real life where body and mind interact. They used survey data from 7,093 patients.

Their correlated physical and mental scores had a correlation of 0.62, showing the two overlap strongly. The new method produced far fewer negative scoring weights, a quirk that caused confusing results before. Similar results held for the shorter SF-12 version. The authors recommend reporting the correlated scores alongside the standard ones. That pairing should reduce contradictions between scale scores and summary scores.
europmc-pmc2077865:
Haring and co-workers presented an optimised chromatin immunoprecipitation protocol in 2007, a method shortened to ChIP. ChIP uses antibodies to find where proteins and chemical marks sit on DNA. It is central to studying gene regulation, but setting it up in new organisms is hard. Data analysis and normalisation are often undervalued, hurting quality. The team built and tested their protocol in maize.

They propose built-in controls for active and for repressed chromatin, DNA regions in on and off states. They argue that quantitative PCR is crucial for high-quality results. Different ways of normalising the data had a major impact on quality, so they compare each approach's strengths and drawbacks. The strategy can be adapted systematically to any tissue type.
europmc-pmc2124965: A medical paper on studies in ferment action and leucocytic proteolysis. The white cells' digestion. This article preserves that biochemistry. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125165: A medical paper studying ferments and ferment-inhibiting substances in tuberculous caseous matter. The TB chemistry. This article preserves that biochemistry. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125265: A medical paper with a new rapid method for isolating tubercle bacilli. The TB germ, caught. This article preserves that bacteriology. It awaits future readers. It retains its place in time. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125765: A medical paper on the cyclic changes in the mammary gland under normal and pathological conditions. The breast's cycles. This article preserves that histology. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it.
europmc-pmc2131065: A medical paper on microbic virulence and host susceptibility in paratyphoid infection. The germ's strength. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131565: A medical paper on the rapid shallow breathing resulting from pulmonary congestion and edema. The labored breath. This article preserves that pulmonology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2374965:
Wright and colleagues searched for cancer stem cells in mouse breast tumors in 2008. Cancer stem cells are a small set of tumor cells thought to seed regrowth and resist drugs. The tumors lacked Brca1, a gene whose inherited faults cause human breast cancer, and the team made 16 cell lines from five such tumors.

Lines from one tumor were rich in cells marked CD44 positive and CD24 negative, the known human breast cancer stem cell pattern. Lines from another carried 2% to 5.9% of cells marked CD133 instead, a second stem marker. As few as 50 to 100 marked cells quickly grew tumors in mice, while unmarked cells needed 50 to 100 times more cells. The marked cells also resisted DNA-damaging drugs, but a heat-shock blocker drug made them sensitive again.
europmc-pmc2453765:
Smitten, Simon, Hochberg, and Suissa pooled studies of cancer in rheumatoid arthritis in 2008. Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the joints, and its treatments suppress the immune system, raising fears of extra cancer risk. The team combined 21 publications reporting standardised incidence ratios, which compare patients with the general public.

Overall cancer incidence was barely raised, at a ratio of 1.05 in the pooled estimate. The picture split sharply by site. Lymphoma, a cancer of immune cells, ran about double the public rate, at 2.08, and lung cancer was raised to 1.63 in the same measure. Colorectal cancer went the other way, at 0.77, and breast cancer at 0.84, both below public rates. Hodgkin lymphoma carried a higher excess than the non-Hodgkin kind.
europmc-pmc2621365:
Bernhart, Hofacker, Will, Gruber, and Stadler released an improved RNAalifold in 2008. The program is widely used. It predicts the shared folded shape of a set of related RNA molecules. RNA folds into structures that determine its function, and comparing sequences helps pin the true fold. Users and rival methods had exposed weaknesses in the original tool's handling of gaps and scoring.

The new version treats alignment gaps in a more rational way. It also replaces the simple covariance scoring with RIBOSUM-like matrices. Those matrices weight likely base-pair exchanges. Accuracy improved substantially without slowing the program down. On several test data sets the updated tool beat not only its predecessor but also competing approaches based on grammars, expected accuracy, and classifiers. The authors say it can replace the old version for almost any application.
europmc-pmc2654865:
Stark and Savarirayan reviewed in 2009 osteopetrosis, a family of rare inherited disorders in which bones grow too dense. The name means marble bone disease. The fault lies in osteoclasts, the cells that normally break bone down as the skeleton renews itself. When they fail, old bone piles up instead of being recycled.

Forms range from lethal to harmless. The severe recessive form strikes about one baby in 250,000 and can cause fractures, seizures from low calcium, and bone marrow failure. A milder dominant form, at one in 20,000 births, may show only late fractures or be found by chance on an X-ray. Faults in at least ten genes explain about 70 percent of cases. Diagnosis rests on scans and symptoms, confirmed by gene tests where possible, and guides treatment and family advice.
europmc-pmc2658865:
Belch led a trial in 2008 for the Prevention of Progression of Arterial Disease and Diabetes Study Group. It tested whether aspirin or antioxidant pills protect people with diabetes and silent leg artery disease. The 1,276 Scottish adults had narrowed leg arteries shown by a pressure test, but no symptoms yet. Each person got aspirin, antioxidants, both, or dummy pills.

After follow-up, heart attacks, strokes, deaths, and amputations struck the groups at nearly the same rates. About 18 percent in each arm suffered a main event. Aspirin showed no benefit, and neither did the antioxidant mix, and taking both together changed nothing. Deaths from heart disease or stroke were, if anything, slightly higher with aspirin. The trial argues against giving these pills to diabetic patients who feel well, at least for this silent stage of artery disease.
europmc-pmc2680965:
Nevin and colleagues asked in 2009 how a bacterium passes electric current through thick films of itself to an electrode. Geobacter sulfurreducens can breathe onto graphite, dumping electrons outside its body, a trick used in microbe-powered fuel cells. Films over 50 micrometers thick still conduct, but the wiring was a mystery.

Films grown on electrodes differed sharply from films grown on the same surface with a chemical breathing partner instead. Gene readings found 13 genes turned up in the current-making films. Two stood out most: one for hair-like pili, and one for a surface protein called OmcZ. Deleting either the pilus gene or the OmcZ gene wrecked both current output and film building, while deleting three related surface proteins did not. The electrode-grown film, the authors conclude, is built and wired specifically for exporting electrons.
europmc-pmc2685765:
Lanone and co-authors compared in 2009 the toxicity of 24 manufactured nanoparticles on two human lung cell lines. Nanoparticles, specks thousands of times thinner than a hair, go into sunscreens, coatings, and electronics. Workers and users breathe them, yet safety data lagged behind production. The team wanted both a ranking of danger and a fast standard test.

They exposed lung surface cells and immune cells to particles of matched size but different chemistry, and read survival with two assays at two time points. The most sensitive setup paired one assay with the immune cells at 24 hours. Copper and zinc particles killed the most cells. Titanium, aluminum, cerium, and zirconium oxides sat in the middle. Tungsten carbide showed no toxicity at all. Neither particle size nor surface area predicted the harm; chemistry did.
europmc-pmc2686165:
Gispert and a large team studied in 2009 aged mice missing PINK1, a mitochondria protein whose loss causes an inherited form of Parkinson disease in people. They bred the knockout mice and watched them into old age, looking for the movement disorder's signs.

Old mice without PINK1 moved less in spontaneous activity and lost weight progressively, echoing the human illness. Dopamine, the brain chemical that fails in Parkinson disease, ran abnormal in the key pathway. Yet the expected cell death did not appear: no neurons died in that pathway, and no Lewy bodies, the protein clumps of the human disease, formed. Life span was normal too. Inside the cells, though, mitochondria failed step by step. Their protein imports slowed, and their energy making and breathing weakened. Only under stress did the organelles clump oddly. The model, the authors say, captures Parkinson disease's slow power failure without the final cell death.
europmc-pmc2724665:
Uttara, Singh, Zamboni, and Mahajan reviewed in 2009 how oxidative stress drives nerve cell loss in diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, and what antioxidant therapies might do. Free radicals are a normal by-product of oxygen use, but excess reactive oxygen species injure proteins, DNA, and tissues. The brain is especially exposed because nerve cells rely heavily on oxygen.

Their review covers upstream options that cut radical production and downstream options that mop radicals up after they form. Antioxidants from diet and medicinal herbs can also bind metal ions involved in plaque formation, a process tied to Alzheimer's damage. They frame antioxidant therapy as a promising route to slow post-stress degeneration, while noting the need for proven treatments.
europmc-pmc2725865:
Witte, Strommenger, Stanek, and Cuny reported in 2007 that methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus of lineage ST398 occurs in both humans and animals in Central Europe. This drug-resistant bacterium, called MRSA, was long a hospital problem, and cases in livestock and pets were rare. Whether the same lineage passes between animals and people was an open question.

Typing isolates from sporadic infections in people, horses, and other animals in Germany and Austria showed the ST398 isolates were genetically related across species. That close match supports shared circulation between human and animal hosts, rather than separate lineages. The finding adds farm and veterinary settings to the map of MRSA spread that control programs must watch.
europmc-pmc2732465:
Coker and co-authors reviewed in 2002 human campylobacteriosis in developing countries, gut infection by Campylobacter bacteria, mainly the species jejuni and coli. The germ is among those most often found in stool of infants with diarrhea in poorer countries, usually from contaminated food or water. Research and control had focused far more on developed countries, where case counts were also rising.

They contrast the disease patterns in developing and developed settings, including age patterns, repeat exposure, and the added risk of HIV-related deaths. Most developing countries lack national surveillance for this infection, so its true burden stays blurred. They call for national programs and international partnerships to close the knowledge gaps and guide control.
europmc-pmc2743365:
Ueno and co-authors ran a phase three trial in 2009 testing whether gemcitabine chemotherapy after surgery helps patients with resected pancreatic cancer. Surgery is the only chance of cure, yet recurrence is very high and five-year survival after resection is low. One hundred nineteen patients with a complete-appearing resection and no prior drug or radiation treatment were randomized in Japan.

Half received gemcitabine in three cycles and half had surgery alone. Disease-free survival was significantly longer with the drug, with median values of about eleven months versus five months, and blood toxicity was common but mostly brief. Overall survival did not differ significantly, at about twenty-two versus eighteen months. Adjuvant gemcitabine thus delays recurrence after curative resection.
europmc-pmc2815665:
Kabsch described the XDS software package in 2010, a standard tool for turning raw X-ray diffraction images into data that reveals crystal structure. Diffraction is the scatter pattern a crystal makes under X-rays, and rotation images are frames taken while the crystal slowly turns. The package grew from his earlier work dating to the late nineteen eighties.

Three programs split the job. The main one reads a run of images, infers the crystal's symmetry, and lists corrected spot strengths nearly automatically. A second program puts separate runs on one scale and corrects for beam damage and absorption, while a third converts the results into formats other structure programs accept. The workflow runs as eight file-linked steps that can be rerun singly.
europmc-pmc2855365:
Srinivasan and colleagues tracked vaginal bacteria day by day in 2010 to see how much the mix shifts in healthy women and how it answers treatment in bacterial vaginosis. Twenty-two women gave daily samples for up to two weeks, measured by targeted DNA tests for eleven key bacteria. Women with vaginosis received five days of metronidazole gel.

Healthy women's protective lactobacilli swung sharply across the monthly cycle: two key species fell as Gardnerella vaginalis rose at period onset. In treated women the vaginosis bacteria crashed below detection within days. In women whose condition returned, the same bacteria first crashed then rebounded, which argues against drug resistance and points instead to re-seeding or regrowth from a hidden reservoir.
europmc-pmc2861665:
Leung and Cahill reviewed in 2010 how an immune signal called TNF-alpha may drive neuropathic pain, the burning pain that follows nerve damage. Such pain often outlasts the injury and can feel far stronger than the trigger warrants. TNF-alpha was first known as an immune messenger, but it also acts inside the nervous system.

Animal studies using many kinds of nerve injury place TNF-alpha at the center of pain sensitization, in both the injured nerve and the spinal cord. Signals interacting with it, including a stress pathway in cells, form a web that keeps pain switched on. Yet human trials of anti-TNF drugs for sciatica have largely failed, so the authors argue future drugs should target the wider web, not the single signal.
europmc-pmc2864565:
Robinson and Oshlack presented in 2010 a scaling method that made RNA sequencing data far more trustworthy for comparing gene activity. RNA-seq counts RNA copies gene by gene, but samples differ in total output and a few loud genes can skew every comparison. Their method, trimmed mean of M values, rescales each sample using the bulk of genes rather than the extremes.

The authors show that simple total-count scaling can invent false differences or hide real ones when a sample's mix of active genes shifts. Their rescaling removes that bias in both test data and real experiments. The method became a standard step in widely used analysis software, and it underpins countless later studies that hunt for genes switched on or off in disease.
europmc-pmc2917065:
Ku and colleagues reported in 2010 their hospital's early experience giving ipilimumab, an immune-releasing antibody, to advanced melanoma patients under compassionate use. The drug blocks CTLA-4, a brake on T cells, and the patients had run out of standard options. Memorial Sloan-Kettering treated this refractory group and tracked who lived longest against simple blood measures.

One routine measure stood out: the absolute lymphocyte count after two doses. Patients whose counts ran higher at that early checkpoint survived significantly longer than those whose counts stayed low. The count costs nothing extra, since it rides on standard blood work, yet it separates likely beneficiaries weeks into therapy. An early, cheap biomarker is precious for an expensive drug with delayed effects, and the authors propose it for prospective testing.
europmc-pmc2935965:
Hawley and co-authors used engineered cells in 2010 to sort out the many ways drugs and stresses switch on AMPK, a protein that senses low cell energy. Lots of agents activate it, yet their routes often stayed unclear.

Cells carrying a normal gamma subunit were compared with cells carrying a variant blind to AMP. Poisons that block mitochondria, plus metformin and several other agents, worked only in normal cells and also drained cell energy. Other triggers, including a calcium-raising agent and osmotic stress, worked in both lines. The tests separate at least six activation routes.
europmc-pmc2987465:
Boulon and co-authors reviewed how the nucleolus, the cell nucleus's ribosome factory, responds to stress in a 2010 article. Cells answer stress fast, pausing growth programmes and switching on repair, often reshaping their nuclear compartments.

The nucleolus senses trouble and helps coordinate the reply, including control of p53, a guardian protein that can halt the cell cycle or trigger cell death. Stress alters the nucleolus's shape, contents, and output in characteristic ways. The review also covers its partner compartment, the Cajal body, and how the two exchange components during stress responses.
europmc-pmc3018565:
Cuzick and the UK/ANZ trial team reported long-term results in 2011. The trial tested radiotherapy and the hormone drug tamoxifen after surgery. Patients had ductal carcinoma in situ, a contained early breast lesion. Early results favoured radiotherapy, with tamoxifen unclear.

Women whose lesion was fully cut out entered a two-by-two randomised trial testing each treatment independently. Over long follow-up, radiotherapy cut new events in the same breast, both invasive cancer and further in-situ disease. Tamoxifen's comparison covered any new breast event, including the other breast. The mature data guide how hard to treat a lesion that may never progress.
europmc-pmc3060065:
Perelman and a large team built in 2011 a family tree of living primates from fresh genome data on a broad scale. They gathered about eight million DNA letters from nearly two hundred primates spanning most known genera, plus relatives from neighboring mammal orders for comparison. Primate classification had long been tangled and disputed, which hampered work from human evolution to conservation.

The resulting tree was unusually firm and cleared up many disputed branchings. It also revealed hidden patterns: species still splitting today, family lines shaped by past interbreeding, ancient relic lineages, and uneven rates of change and of DNA insertions between branches. For humans, the tree sharpens the timeline of our own lineage. The authors offer it as a shared framework for studying adaptation, emerging diseases, and which primate species most need protection.
europmc-pmc3060165:
Cheng and colleagues reported in 2011 that a tiny RNA measured in blood plasma can flag colon cancer that has spread, and predicts how patients will fare. Blood markers that are sensitive and noninvasive are badly needed for this common cancer. The team measured three candidate microRNAs in plasma from patients and healthy donors, focusing on the one called miR-141.

Levels of that RNA were clearly higher in patients whose cancer had reached the distant spread stage. Pairing it with the standard blood marker used for this cancer improved detection further. The pattern held up in a second, independent patient group from another city. High levels also predicted shorter survival in both groups and stood as an independent warning sign. Oddly, tumor tissue itself showed no such difference, hinting the blood signal may come from the body's wider response.
europmc-pmc3081065:
Brown and a large team reported in 2011 that broken copies of a skin barrier gene sharply raise the risk of peanut allergy. The gene makes filaggrin, a protein that helps skin hold its barrier, and broken copies were already known to drive eczema and related allergies. The team compared patients with challenge proven peanut allergy against large control groups in Britain, Ireland, and the Netherlands, then repeated the test in Canada.

Carrying a broken copy multiplied the odds of peanut allergy several fold in the first study, and the link held in the Canadian group. It stayed significant even after accounting for eczema, so it is not just a side effect of skin disease. The result points to a leaky barrier as a root step in food allergy, perhaps letting peanut proteins in through skin. It also suggests barrier repair could become a prevention strategy.
europmc-pmc3119065:
Zheng Wei Lee and colleagues tested a slow-release gas donor against cancer in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The gas, hydrogen sulfide, is made in the body in small amounts, and quick-acting donors fade within an hour. Their compound instead leaks the gas at low levels for days, which let them ask what steady exposure does to tumour cells.

The donor killed all seven human cancer cell lines tested, including liver, breast, and blood cancers, while sparing normal lung cells. A twin compound that cannot release the gas did nothing, proving the gas itself was the active part. Treated cancer cells showed signs of self-destruction and stalled division, and tumours grown in mice shrank notably over two weeks. The authors propose such donors as a fresh class of cancer drug candidates.
europmc-pmc3139665:
Sydney Rosen and Matthew Fox reviewed what happens between HIV testing and treatment in sub-Saharan Africa in a 2011 paper in PLoS Medicine. Millions had gained access to life-extending drugs, yet many patients still arrived for treatment dangerously late. The authors gathered the few studies tracking patients who tested positive but were not yet eligible for drug therapy.

Fewer than a third of such patients stayed in care continuously until treatment could start. People drifted away at linking, monitoring, and return visits, often reappearing only when seriously ill, with immune counts far below even old treatment thresholds. The review argues that retention before treatment deserves the same attention as retention on it, and that better tracking systems are needed to find and fix the leaks.
europmc-pmc3163565:
Bo Li and Colin Dewey presented software for measuring gene activity from RNA sequencing in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. The hard part is reads that match several genes or several versions of one gene, which naive counting misassigns. Their program distributes such shared reads by probability and reports uncertainty ranges for each estimate.

Uniquely, the tool needs no reference genome, so it pairs with freshly assembled transcript sets for species whose genomes were never sequenced. On simulated and real data it matched or beat genome-based rivals. Experiments with its simulation feature yielded design advice. Gene-level estimates favour many short single reads, while sorting versions within a gene can benefit from reads taken from both fragment ends. The package is user-friendly and free.
europmc-pmc3248465:
Laia Navarro-Martín and colleagues found an epigenetic switch behind temperature-driven sex ratios in the European sea bass, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. In this fish, warmer early development yields more males, well before the gonads form, and the mechanism was unknown. The key gene makes aromatase, the enzyme that converts male hormones into estrogens.

Juvenile males carried about twice the DNA methylation of females on that gene's promoter, the switch region controlling its activity, and methylation ran opposite to expression. Warmth raised promoter methylation in females, masculinizing them, and the effect appeared in the gonads but not the brain, even before sex was set. In test tubes, methylating the promoter stopped two activator proteins from switching the gene on. One temperature-sensitive spot is conserved across species, hinting at a general mechanism.
europmc-pmc3276165:
Bryan Howie, Jonathan Marchini, and Matthew Stephens developed a framework for genotype imputation with thousands of reference genomes, in this 2011 paper in G3. Imputation fills in unmeasured genetic variants in a study by copying from densely typed reference panels, boosting the power of association studies. As projects like 1000 Genomes made panels huge and diverse, choosing which reference haplotypes to use became a bottleneck.

Their approximation sidesteps panel selection: for each study chromosome and each genome region, local sequence similarity picks a custom set of the most useful reference haplotypes on the fly. That keeps computation manageable while using all available references, and it sharpens accuracy at low-frequency variants by catching unexpected sharing between populations. Tests on HapMap data and African malaria-network data showed accurate results across many populations. The method ships in the IMPUTE2 package.
europmc-pmc3279365:
Marta Navarrete and colleagues showed that astrocytes, the brain's support cells, actively help store information, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Biology. Astrocytes were long cast as housekeeping cells for neurons, feeding and cleaning up around them. A newer view, the tripartite synapse, gives them a speaking role in synaptic signaling, and this study tested that role in the living brain.

Combining experiments in living mice with work in tissue preparations, the team examined synapses in the hippocampus, a center for memory. They found that astrocytes mediate a form of synaptic strengthening triggered by cholinergic signaling, the system engaged by attention-related transmitters. Without the astrocytes' participation, that plasticity did not proceed normally. The authors conclude astrocytes do not merely support information storage in the hippocampus; they take part in it directly.
europmc-pmc3292965:
Negrini led an international society of scoliosis specialists in updating treatment guidelines, published in 2012. The society, known as SOSORT, had issued its first guidance in 2005 for curved spines in growing children and teens. Members from many professions, plus a methods expert and a patient representative, reviewed the literature and debated drafts before agreeing on the final text at a 2011 meeting in Barcelona.

The guidelines give sixty five recommendations covering braces, targeted exercises, other non surgical treatments, breathing work, sports, and patient assessment. Braces and assessment draw the most recommendations. The authors are candid that strong research evidence is scarce in this field, with no recommendation backed by the highest grade of evidence, and they invite better studies.
europmc-pmc3302865:
Gallo, Tandon, Alevizos, and Illei tested where tiny regulatory RNAs in blood and saliva actually ride, in a 2012 study. These microRNAs are promising disease markers because they are easy to collect from body fluids, but it was unclear whether they float freely or travel packaged. The team separated tiny membrane parcels called exosomes from human serum and saliva and compared RNA amounts in each fraction.

Most of the measured microRNAs sat inside the exosome fraction rather than the leftover fluid. Some markers appeared only in exosomes and were missed entirely in whole serum. The authors advise future marker studies to start from exosomes, since skipping that step risks missing scarce signals and reporting false negative results.
europmc-pmc3304165:
Tao and co-authors reviewed how small wearable sensors can measure the way people walk, in a 2012 article. Watching gait helps doctors diagnose illness, guide recovery after injury, and judge sports performance, but lab based camera systems are costly and fixed in place. Sensors worn on the body promise the same information anywhere, at low cost.

The review first explains the phases of a step, then surveys the sensors available, including motion sensors and pressure sensors. It sorts analysis methods into those measuring body movement, ground forces, and muscle activity. Applications in clinics, rehabilitation, and sport are summarized separately. The authors expect wearable gait analysis to take a growing role in everyday medical practice as sensors and software improve.
europmc-pmc3318765:
Fleming and Dolan reviewed the brain basis of knowing how well you are performing, in a 2012 article. In any skill, people differ not only in how accurate they are, but also in how well their self judgments track that accuracy. Someone can be good at a task yet poor at sensing their own errors, or the reverse, and this self awareness is called metacognitive ability.

Evidence from memory and decision research shows that self awareness varies widely between people and can separate cleanly from task skill. Brain studies point to the front side areas of the prefrontal cortex, behind the forehead, as key for looking back and judging past performance. Judgments about future performance seem to lean on more central frontal areas instead. The authors sketch how these regions may work with inner body sensing areas to produce accurate self judgments.
europmc-pmc3349865:
Sollid and fellow immunologists proposed a shared naming system for the gluten fragments that drive coeliac disease. Research groups had described T-cell epitopes from wheat, barley, and rye proteins under inconsistent labels, making results hard to compare across laboratories and peptide variants.

Their proposal organises epitopes by the HLA-DQ molecule that presents them and the grain protein they derive from, covering the recognised DQ2- and DQ8-restricted sequences. A systematic nomenclature lets researchers state precisely which peptide a study used, including deamidated forms produced by tissue transglutaminase. The authors intend the scheme to tidy a literature central to understanding coeliac disease.
europmc-pmc3361365:
Perše and Cerar examined the dextran sodium sulphate model of colitis, one of the most popular ways to study inflammatory bowel disease in mice. The model is praised for its simplicity: adding the compound to drinking water produces gut inflammation resembling human disease, which makes it attractive for testing mechanisms and therapies.

The authors warn that the model's simplicity hides traps. Outcomes shift with the dose and molecular weight of the compound, the mouse strain, the gut microbes present, and husbandry conditions. Two laboratories can therefore obtain conflicting results from seemingly identical protocols. Their paper catalogues these variables and offers practical guidance for designing experiments and interpreting results consistently.
europmc-pmc3368265:
Maurer and co-workers asked in 2012 how certain proteins find the growing ends of microtubules, the hollow rails inside cells. End-binding proteins, called EBs, home in on those tips and pull other factors along with them. Nobody knew what feature of the tip they actually recognized.

Using cryo-electron microscopy and glowing-tag imaging, the team built a near-atomic model of the yeast EB protein Mal3 bound to a tip. Its grip bridges the tube's strands and sits beside the spot where the fuel molecule GTP is exchanged. That position lets it sense the tip's chemical state. The same region also caps the tube and guards it from falling apart.
europmc-pmc3409365:
Smink, van Hoeken, and Hoek reviewed in 2012 how often eating disorders occur and how deadly they are. The team searched the major medical databases for studies on incidence, prevalence, and mortality. Eating disorders are uncommon overall, but their patterns differ sharply by type, age, and sex.

Anorexia nervosa occurs fairly often among young women, and new cases in girls aged fifteen to nineteen have risen even as the overall rate held steady. Bulimia nervosa, by contrast, may have declined since the early nineteen nineties. Binge eating disorder is the most common of the group among men and older adults. All these disorders raise the risk of death, anorexia most starkly.
europmc-pmc3424165:
Cornman and co-workers surveyed honey bee colonies across the United States in 2012 to see which germs haunt collapsing colonies. Colony Collapse Disorder empties hives with unusual speed and spread, sometimes without signs of known disease. The team measured the presence and load of known bee pathogens in collapsing, weak, and strong colonies.

Collapsing colonies carried more kinds of pathogens, and in greater amounts, than healthy ones. Pathogen loads rose and fell together in collapsing hives but not in controls, hinting that infections either pile onto weakened bees or amplify each other. Deep RNA sequencing found new strains of Lake Sinai viruses and a shifted gut bacterial mix that may mark the disorder. Germ teamwork, they argue, belongs at the center of the story.

europmc-pmc9718665: Pachitariu and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on cellpose 2-0: how to train your own model. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9806465: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on cerebral small vessel disease: recent advances (new steps forward) and future directions. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
frus-1861-d165:
Horace Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 June 1861. Perry served the American legation in Madrid. The dispatch is document 165 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Legation staff kept the post running between ministers and during absences. Perry's reports from Madrid gave Washington a steady line on Spain. His June letter shows the second tier of the service at work, far from the famous names. Staff men like Perry rarely signed the great notes, yet the record keeps their names. Names of staff men in the headings honor work that great notes often hide.
frus-1861-d265:
A State Department letter of 2 November 1861 told James Shepherd Pike what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 265 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the autumn of the war's first year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d65:
Writing from London on 2 August 1861, Charles Francis Adams laid the post Bull Run picture before Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 65 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

August brought the full weight of the Bull Run defeat to London opinion. Adams reported how ministers and papers now sized up the Union's strength. His letter helped Seward judge how much firmness the British would bear, and how much they would test. Cotton, credit, and pride all pulled London toward the South in that bleak month. Each of those pulls can be felt in the wary tone of his August pages.
frus-1862-d165:
Two Seward letters to London bear the date 20 October 1862, and this one is Document 165 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, received it at the legation in London.

Splitting one day's business into two letters let clerks file each topic apart and let the envoy answer point by point. It also means no single letter holds the whole picture for that date. Read with its same-day pair and the reports Adams sent back, this dispatch helps rebuild a week of Anglo-American dealings in full. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d265:
Dated 8 April 1862, Document 265 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It appears in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward wrote the day after Shiloh's second day ended in Tennessee, though full news had not yet settled. Battles of that scale moved foreign markets and ministries within days. A dispatch sent in their wake carried Washington's framing of events to Paris before French papers fixed their own version, which was half its purpose. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d365:
On 20 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, in a letter printed as Document 365 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward's May letters to Mercier came in the season when France, checked at Puebla, was deciding how deep its Mexican venture would go. Washington's interest was plain: a France busy in Mexico had less freedom to aid the South. The letter is part of the careful spring exchange in which each side measured the other's intentions. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d465:
George Perkins Marsh in Turin received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 September 1862. It is Document 465 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote four days before Antietam, in the same mid-September round of orders that went to Vienna, Madrid, and The Hague. Marsh's Italy had just been shaken by Garibaldi's clash with royal troops at Aspromonte, news that filled his reports that season. The instruction kept the Turin legation aligned with Washington's line as the war reached its autumn crisis. Small posts received the same careful handling as great ones in Seward's system, and this letter is proof of it.
frus-1862-d565:
Henry Shelton Sanford wrote from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 March 1862. His report is Document 565 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

By March 1862 Union victories in the West had improved the American position in Europe, and Sanford's reports tracked the change from his crossroads post. Belgium's industries felt the war through lost American trade, and its court watched France's Mexican venture with concern. Sanford also kept watch on Confederate agents working in Europe, a duty he pursued with zeal. His spring letter is one of the steady reports by which Washington measured opinion in the smaller capitals that autumn's councils would consult.
frus-1862-d65:
Seward heard from Charles Francis Adams on 15 May 1862, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 65 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d665:
The President of the United States sent this formal letter to the Tycoon of Japan on 1 August 1861. Tycoon was the name American papers used for the shogun, Japan's military ruler. The letter, signed in President Abraham Lincoln's name, is document 665 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Heads of state wrote such letters on great matters of friendship and form, and envoys bore them by hand. This one kept up the bond that Commodore Perry's visit and Townsend Harris's treaty had made in the 1850s. It stands out in the file: amid piles of desk mail, here is the top of both governments speaking at once.
frus-1863p1-d165:
Late April brought this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams in London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 23 April 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 165 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-April mail from London took stock of a spring that had gone the Union's way on the ships. Adams still watched the yards and the courts, since one held raider did not end the trade. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day. It shows the legation's watch kept at full care even as the news grew kind.
frus-1863p1-d265:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 August 1863. It is document 265 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d365:
From the British legation in Washington on 19 January 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 365 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Lyons reported each exchange to Lord John Russell in London. What he wrote to Seward, and what Seward answered, shaped British choices about the war. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d465:
A 16 April 1863 dispatch from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington reached William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d565:
Document 565 in the volume is a letter of 16 June 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d65:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 January 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume bears the same date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 65 in part one of the 1863 volume.

The last days of January kept the legation busy with Britain's reading of the war. Adams tracked the press, the public meetings, and the moves of Southern men in London. His reports reached Washington about ten days after he wrote them. This dispatch is one of a same-day pair, part of the near-weekly flow that made the London file the spine of the volume.
frus-1863p1-d665:
The 16 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

The value of the London file is its view from inside Britain: cabinet moods, press talk, and opinion's turn after Gettysburg and Vicksburg. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d165: Secretary Hull set down a memorandum on October 25, 1943, during the Moscow Conference, and it is Document 165 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It shares its date with his other memorandum in the main sequence, a sign of how much paper the conference's middle days produced. The record gives the author and the date and no topic. Hull's paper is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the Moscow documents.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d265:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 24 November 1943, at half past two in the afternoon, open with a warm exchange over Thanksgiving. Sir Alan Brooke had arranged for a service in Cairo cathedral the next evening, and Admiral Leahy accepted the British invitation with thanks on behalf of the American chiefs.

The main business is machinery for cooperation with the Soviet Union and China, under papers C.C.S. 406 and 406/1. Brooke argues that a standing United Chiefs of Staff with real power would sit awkwardly above the combined body, since Russia and China fight different enemies. The chiefs agree to propose nothing themselves, to resist a standing committee if pressed, and for now to invite Soviet and Chinese officers to conference sessions touching their own concerns.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d365:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a meeting between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin at Tehran on 29 November 1943, at a quarter to three in the afternoon. Much of it is Roosevelt handing over papers and opening the question of the postwar peace organization.

Roosevelt lends Stalin a report by an American officer who spent six months with Tito in Yugoslavia. He also gives him papers on shuttle-bombing bases in Russia. More papers cover air and naval planning against Japan. Throughout, he stresses the strictest secrecy. He then sketches his world organization: a large United Nations body making recommendations, and a smaller executive committee of the Big Four plus six other states, handling non-military questions. Stalin probes whether that committee could bind nations, noting it could in fact force compliance, and Roosevelt agrees.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d465:
Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's closest aide, wrote to Soviet foreign commissar Vyacheslav Molotov on December 2, 1943, the day after the Tehran Conference closed. Hopkins had been at Roosevelt's side through the first meeting with Stalin. The State Department later printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A direct Hopkins-to-Molotov line was one of the warmest channels between Washington and Moscow, built on Hopkins's earlier missions to the Soviet Union. Coming straight after Tehran, the message belongs to the work of holding the new three-way partnership together. It shows diplomacy carried on by trusted envoys rather than formal notes between foreign offices.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d565:
Harry Dexter White of the Treasury wrote a second memorandum on August 15, 1944, two days after the first. Back-to-back papers from the same official usually mean a subject being worked through in stages. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

White served Secretary Morgenthau as his chief assistant on international money questions, the field where the postwar settlement was furthest advanced. August 1944 also brought the liberation of Paris and planning for the Quebec Conference in September. For readers, paired White memoranda show the Treasury developing its positions in writing, ready to be argued when the leaders met again.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d65: On October 27, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, the day after the busiest letter day of the Moscow season. His message is Document 65 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Moscow Conference was ending, and attention in both capitals was turning to the leaders' own meetings. The record gives the date and the two names. The message rests in the Foreign Relations volume for readers to weigh in sequence.
frus-1944-quebec-d165:
Hull sent Roosevelt this top-secret memorandum, "Indochina and Southeast Asia," on September 8, 1944. France sought restoration of Indochina and had promised reforms, while fearing Chinese ambitions. Britain, Hull reported, had swung behind restoring French authority, partly to strengthen its own claim to Hong Kong. British agents were already training French officers and had dropped a de Gaullist agent into Indochina.

Against restoration, the memo urges early, dramatic announcements by the nations concerned. It proposes specific dates for independence or self-government, steps to build native capacity to rule, and pledges of economic equality. Such commitments, it argues, would win the goodwill of Southeast Asia's peoples, save Allied lives, and serve American postwar interests in trade and security.
frus-1944-quebec-d265:
Personnel shipping after the European war is the subject of C.C.S. 675, a British Chiefs' memorandum of September 12, 1944. Once hostilities in Europe ended, the global movement of men would be enormous and complex. Troops would need to move to the Pacific, home for demobilization, and between theaters, all competing for the same ships at the same moment.

Decisions on priorities among those movements would be necessary, the paper argues. It recommends an immediate examination of the problem's scope and of available shipping resources. The service departments of both countries would conduct it, working with the shipping authorities. The discussion that day sent General Somervell to confer with Lord Leathers.
frus-1944-quebec-d65:
