A second message from Prime Minister Churchill to President Roosevelt bears the date September 12, 1944, the Quebec Conference's opening day. The State Department printed both in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Opening days generate paper: welcomes, agenda points, and first positions all need recording. Churchill's two messages show him settling into the conference in his characteristic way, writing his way into the argument before the sessions could do it for him. For readers, the pair conveys the tempo of day one at Quebec, when two governments began dividing the end of a world war.
frus-1945-50-intel-d165:
A letter from the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Hoover) reached the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) on 23 August 1946. Readers meet it as document 165 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

A formal letter was a step above a memo: it put a request or a stance on record under the writer's signature. Read in sequence, the letters show two offices testing how far each could push the other. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d265:
A memorandum dated 1 April 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Office of Information and Educational Exchange (Stone). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 265 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d365:
On 11 February 1949, Robert Blum of the Office of the Secretary of Defense sent a letter to Allen W. Dulles. It is document 365 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The first Dulles Report season had begun: an outside team judged the CIA while the agency and its partners answered back.

The text is one side of an exchange, set out in full under the writer's own name and title. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d65:
Arnold Miles of the Budget Bureau wrote to a bureau colleague, Hoelscher, on 3 January 1946. The new year opened with the intelligence settlement nearly ripe. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Budget Bureau staff papers in January 1946 belong to the drafting of the president's directive and the money that would follow it. Miles, who had written inside the bureau the day before the OSS order, appears again at the matching moment of creation. Readers who follow the bureau's thread see its quiet power whole. It was present at the death of the old agency. It was present at the birth of the new arrangement alike.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d165:
“Suggested United States Policy Regarding Poland” heads this briefing book paper, prepared for the President's trip and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary states the line Roosevelt's team meant to hold at the Big Three table.

The aim is a Poland ruled in time by a truly democratic government of the people's own choice. No stopgap regime should be allowed to harden into permanence before the people's will can show itself. So Washington should not recognize the Lublin provisional government on present proof. It should press for a leading role for the Peasant Party and for Mikolajczyk in any interim plans. Elections, when they come, should be watched under United Nations arrangements the United States would sponsor.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d265:
Washington briefed General Deane for his last Moscow talks before the conference on 18 January 1945. The Joint Chiefs' cable, WAR 23255, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It sets tight limits on what the head of the Moscow military mission may say.

Deane is to ask, without any hint of commitment, whether Russia will need trans-Pacific aid once she enters the war. He is to warn that opening sea routes to the Okhotsk and Amur ports would be costly. It would draw strength from the drive on Japan from the south. Amphibious moves in the North Pacific in 1945 are remote. Any route forced open must serve the earliest defeat of Japan. The two air forces' combined strength should be used early and hard.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d365: Admiral Leahy wrote to General Antonov at Yalta on February 7, 1945, proposing a most secret meeting. The American Chiefs of Staff wished to meet the Soviet chiefs the next day, Thursday, February 8, at 3 p.m. The place would be the Russian headquarters. No one was to be present but the chiefs themselves and one interpreter. The Russian interpreter, Leahy added, would be satisfactory for the American side. The caution is telling: the subject, Soviet entry into the war against Japan, was among the deepest secrets of the conference.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d465:
Decisions, set in order, fill the working draft of the Protocol of Proceedings as revised by the foreign ministers on February 11, 1945. Under world organisation, it was decided to summon a United Nations conference for Wednesday, April 25, 1945. It would be held in the United States of America.

The nations to be invited were listed in two groups. First came the United Nations as they stood on February 8. Then came Associated Nations that declared war on the common enemy by March 1. When the conference met, British and American delegates would back seats for two Soviet republics. The draft is the conference's legal skeleton, before the communiqué clothed it in prose.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d65:
Generals Eisenhower and Alexander should attend Yalta as well as Malta, Churchill argued on 24 January 1945. His telegram to Roosevelt, number 894, is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It concerns who would advise the leaders on military questions.

Churchill warns that if the two commanders come only to Malta, the heads of government cannot enter fully into military problems at Yalta. If the generals must miss one stop, he says, it should be Malta. The editors note the outcome: Alexander attended both meetings, Eisenhower did not, and his chief of staff, Bedell Smith, came to Malta instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d165:
The State Department's Staff Committee drafted its own proposed agenda in a paper dated June 22, 1945. The paper, SC-136, is document 165 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It lists only matters on which the United States wished to take the lead and make firm proposals.

The first item is machinery for the peace settlements, built around the proposed Council of Foreign Ministers. The second covers territorial settlements, transfers of populations, and peace treaties with Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary, with the details referred to the new council. A Germany section begins with the Control Council. Items the British or Soviets might raise are left off the list, though briefing papers on them were being prepared in case of need. The paper is the working draft behind the American program at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d265:
Robert Murphy forwarded Eisenhower's Danube proposal in a telegram from Hoechst on July 5, 1945. The message is document 265 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It points the State Department to SHAEF's message Scaf 471 of July 3, on reopening the Danube and on the river shipping now in American hands.

SHAEF recommends a policy aimed at restoring the river's international character, starting with an interim Danubian navigation agency. Murphy also reports the reply sent to Marshal Tolbukhin's inquiry about the Danube fleet. The reply said seized Allied property was a matter for the governments. It also said a survey of all craft under Allied control was under way. And SHAEF urged the earliest use of the craft for mutual benefit. The message was repeated to Moscow for Pauley and to Caserta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d365:
Stimson answered Grew's letter on western Europe in extracts of a reply dated July 4, 1945. Grew had raised many points about conditions in the freed countries in his letter of June 8. Stimson says he shares the concern over a distressing situation, and he recognizes the weight of the points raised.

The War Department, he assures Grew, will cooperate within its proper sphere. But many of Grew's points, he argues, fall outside the policy in the President's letter of May 21. That policy ended the Army's duty to supply civilians in freed areas once the military task was done. Stimson feared field commanders would otherwise be swallowed by civilian needs.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d465:
Peace terms for Italy are weighed in an undated memorandum by the Joint Strategic Survey Committee. The committee agrees with the Acting Secretary of State that America gains by helping Italy's conversion into a stable, peaceful, and constructive element among the nations of Europe. Some constructive steps, it says, should move Italy away from her present odd position.

The onerous and obsolete surrender terms, the committee argues, no longer fit the situation today. It adds a caution of its own. The State Department was now weighing a permanent settlement of Italian frontiers in Europe and Africa. Negotiations on frontiers, the committee wishes to point out, raise questions that should not be swept into the treaty question carelessly.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d565:
The Acting Secretary of State wired Ambassador Kirk in Italy on June 22, 1945. The urgent secret message is document 565 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Washington was confused about what had in fact been signed at Duino.

The Department had thought all appendices were signed on June 20. Belgrade now said the deals left out article 3 of the Belgrade agreement. Kirk is told to clear this up at once and to send the full text by courier. The wire stresses that article 3 leaves the use of local civil bodies to Field Marshal Alexander's free choice. Rule west of the Morgan Line, it says, must follow the usual Allied pattern, not a purely Yugoslav one.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d65:
Admiral William Leahy, the President's chief of staff, answered Field Marshal Wilson's letter on June 15, 1945. The reply is document 65 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Wilson had proposed that the Combined Chiefs of Staff meet in London for several days before the heads of government gathered in Berlin.

Leahy reports that the U.S. Chiefs of Staff think a London meeting beforehand is unwise. They are willing to stop in London after the Berlin meeting if one is still needed. If the British still have matters to raise early, he suggests using the British Joint Staff Mission in Washington instead, with any visiting British chiefs kept out of the press. The letter shows staff-level friction over how the allies would plan the war's end.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d665:
Tangier talks hit French objections, Ambassador Caffery reported from Paris on July 4, 1945. His second secret wire of the day is document 665 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It records a long talk between the U.S. delegate Villard and a French official, Meyrier.

Meyrier first objected to Washington's account of how the U.S. joined the talks. Any other description than a joint British-U.S. arrangement, he said, put France in an awkward spot. He then warned that admitting the Soviets would force invites to all other statute powers. Belgium had already asked to take part, he noted. He also declared the British draft proposal wholly unacceptable to France. In private, he said he had drafted a French plan under which the U.S. would join the control bodies for a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1065: Ambassador Jefferson Caffery sent this one-line telegram from Paris on July 21, 1945. It answers the Secretary of State's instruction of the day before. Caffery had been asked to propose French participation in supervising the Greek elections, on the model of the letter sent to Molotov. Foreign Minister Bidault, he reports, accepted at once on behalf of the French government. The message went on to Washington and Athens as well. No conditions or reservations are recorded in the brief text.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1165:
Ambassador Kirk reported from Rome on 24 July 1945. His Italy dispatches kept coming through the summit's second week. Each cable updated Washington on the post-Mussolini order taking shape in a country still under Allied oversight.

Rome's politics, its parties, and its dealings with the armies on its soil all mattered to the peace. Kirk watched them at first hand and wrote what he saw. This dispatch is another chapter in that running story. The steady flow, more than any single cable, gave the home office the Italian picture it acted on.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1265:
General Somervell, commanding the Army Service Forces, wrote to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 23 July 1945. His command was the army's supply arm, the machine that kept troops fed and equipped on every front. A report from its chief to the top brass carried the logistics view upward.

Supply facts shaped strategy in 1945 as much as battle plans did. What could be shipped, stored, and landed set the bounds of the possible. This message brought those facts to the chiefs mid-summit. It shows the army's quartermaster-in-chief speaking in his own channel, on the record the chiefs kept.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1365:
John McCloy, the assistant secretary of war, wrote to James Dunn, who chaired the State, War, and Navy Coordinating Committee, on 19 July 1945. McCloy was one of the War Department's most trusted hands. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

McCloy's papers repay attention, since he sat at the crossing of war, law, and politics for years. Writing to the committee's chairman put his point into the one channel built to settle fights among the departments. The message shows the home front of the summit. Senior men in Washington worked the same hard questions as the delegation in Germany. Each side needed the other to finish the job.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-165:
A further set of Cohen notes covers August 1, 1945 at Potsdam. Benjamin Cohen recorded more than one session on the closing day. His parallel notes were printed in the second Potsdam volume. They stand as a second witness beside the set from the same date.

Duplicate witness is a gift to readers. Where two records agree, the ground feels firm. Where they differ, the difference itself teaches caution. Cohen's extra pages show a note-taker working to the last hour. They round out the American account of how the conference's final acts took shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-65:
Thompson's minutes record the plenary session of July 22, 1945, at 5 p.m. at Potsdam. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. The session opened with news from Stalin on Austria.

Stalin announced that the withdrawal of Soviet troops in Austria had begun that day. The troops would pull back about one hundred kilometers, with the movement completed by July 24. Churchill said he was very gratified that the Marshal had so quickly carried out his agreement. The President said he was also appreciative, and Stalin replied that it had merely been their duty. Truman then called on Eden to present the morning's foreign ministers' report. Its first subject was the Yalta declaration on liberated Europe. The U.S. memorandum under debate covered election observation, press facilities, and the control commissions in Rumania, Bulgaria, and Hungary.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d765:
Document 765 is the British text of a draft report by the Economic Subcommittee, dated July 21, 1945. Economic questions sat near Potsdam's core: what Germany would pay, produce, and surrender. Each delegation drafted its own versions. The British draft was kept and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Draft reports from rival hands are gold for readers. Set the British text beside the others and the dispute takes shape. Words about coal, food, and factories carried whole regions' futures. The document shows the economic fight in its working clothes. It reminds readers that the settlement was, in large part, an argument about things and money.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d865:
John J. McCloy, the Assistant Secretary of War, sent this memorandum to Assistant Secretary of State William Clayton on July 20, 1945. Its subject is German interim financing, the money needed to feed occupied Germany. McCloy had read a draft paper for the President and found it incomplete.

McCloy lists five points he wants made plain. War Department funds could cover food imports only through October loadings. Congress had limited the money to preventing disease and starvation. He argues the President must send the Secretary of War a written letter of instructions. Without set standards, he warns, the department cannot judge what funds to request.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d965:
John McCloy, Assistant Secretary of War, wrote to the Secretary of State on July 31, 1945, before leaving Babelsberg to tour the American zone. He had talked with Pauley, Clayton, and Clay about the reparations talks. The Army, he notes, can run Germany under any of the plans under discussion, but he leaves two thoughts behind.

First, any Ruhr sharing formula must cover only surplus gear beyond what a self-supporting German economy needs. Fixing a sum now, before damage is known, risks America having to finance that economy. Second, he urges that Control Council members be given power to decide within agreed policies without referring home. Zhukov, he hears, is ready to act that way.
frus-1964-68v01-d265: A 1964-1968 FRUS editorial note from the Vietnam volume on Johnson's August decisions. The Gulf of Tonkin month. This note provides that background. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
fuhlrott-neanderthal-1865:
Johann Carl Fuhlrott, a school master in Elberfeld, was the man who first saw the worth of the Neanderthal bones. Quarry men found them in a cave in the Neander valley in 1856. This book of 1865 is his full case in German for their great age.

Fuhlrott holds that the bones are fossil, the relics of a race from deep in the past. He sets out the cave, the bones, and the scorn his claim drew from the learned world. The book is the find claim writ large, by the man who stood by it first.
galileo-two-new-sciences-salusbury-1665:
Galileo's Two New Sciences, written in 1638, appears here in Thomas Salusbury's 1665 English translation, Mathematical Discourses Concerning Two New Sciences. Salusbury had planned a full English Galileo; this part survived fire and neglect to reach print. It was the first English form of Galileo's last book.

The discourses treat the strength of beams and materials and the laws of falling bodies and projectiles. Galileo's speakers test claims with thought experiments, such as dropping weights tied together. Salusbury's version, though rough in places, put the founding text of modern mechanics into English within a generation. The Crew translation of 1914 later replaced it for most readers.
gao-gaoreports-b-298865: An Italian joint venture doubled its January 2007 protest — two case numbers, one overseas fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The venture challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Foreign filers get the same fair hearing. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299165: Delaware Resource Group of Oklahoma took its February 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-310065: A formal bid-protest decision from the Government Accountability Office, dated November 21, 2007. These decisions settle disputes when a company challenges how a federal agency awarded a contract — here, a filing by NAC International, Inc. The ruling walks through the legal arguments and explains why the protest was sustained or denied, following the strict procedures Congress set for GAO's contract-review role.
gao-gaoreports-b-310865: This 2008 GAO ruling is about availability of Appropriations for Credit Monitoring Services at Nuclear Regulatory Commission. These rulings interpret appropriations law for federal agencies. It becomes part of the body of federal fiscal law. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-311265: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Hogar Crea, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-400065: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Aquaterra Contracting, Inc. Decided July 14, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-365: Checked-bag machines needed a rollout map in 2005, and GAO's report says the deployment had to be planned well. The review draws the map. The suitcases deserved the smart screening. The map had to be smart. The screening was smart.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-665: Plutonium consolidation needed safe action in 2005, and GAO's report says DOE had to take steps to safely consolidate the material. The findings demand the safety. The report warns that the bomb fuel deserved careful handling. The action had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-865: Job rehab for the disabled needed sharper yardsticks in 2005, and GAO's report says better gauges could lift the program. The findings demand the measures. The report warns that the disabled workers deserved proven help. The disabled workers deserved proven help.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1065: Privatizing tax collection needed care in 2006, and GAO's report says the IRS had to complete steps to ensure contracting out worked. The findings demand the follow-through. The report warns that the for-profit collectors needed firm leashes. The outsourcing had to pay off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-165: False domain name contact info was rampant in 2005, and GAO's report examines the prevalence of bogus registrations. The findings count the fakes. The report warns that the internet's phone book should not lie. The prevalence had to be faced. The internet's phone book should not lie.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-265: Troops-to-Teachers was diversifying classrooms in 2006, and GAO's report says the program brought more men and minorities to teaching, though management could improve. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report warns that the veterans-turned-teachers deserved good management. The management had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-565: Small business research awards got counted in 2006, and GAO's report shares information on NIH and Pentagon awards from 2001 to 2004. The findings do the tally. The report shows the innovation dollars were being tracked. The awards had to be transparent. The innovation dollars were tracked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-765: The government's data quality needed better oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says expanded oversight and clearer guidance could improve the Information Quality Act's results. The findings demand the upgrade. The report warns that the official numbers should be trustworthy. The quality had to be assured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1065: The visitor-tracking system was drifting in 2007 — years old, still no compass. GAO's report says the program meant to log who enters and leaves America lacked direction and sound running. The findings describe a flagship border-tech promise stuck in neutral while the debate over immigration raged around it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-265: Export controls were a tangled web in 2007, and GAO's report says enforcing the inherently complex system stayed hard. The findings map the knots. The report warns that the gates guarding dangerous tech needed stronger hinges. The complexity could not be an excuse.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-465: Food stamp rules for the jobless needed clearer guidance in 2007 — GAO's report says better monitoring would keep the noncash categories honest. The findings press for the playbook. The report's aim: benefits for those who need them, not those who game them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-565: The immigration cops' computers were creaking in 2007 — GAO's report says the agency had to face its infrastructure rot head-on and soon. The findings target the neglected backbone systems in detail. The report's warning stands: you cannot enforce the border on broken machines.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-65: Federal cyber defenses needed regular checkups in 2007, and GAO's report says agencies had to develop policies for periodic testing. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the untested lock was the unlocked lock. The testing had to be routine.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-765: The proxy advisers held quiet power in 2007 — GAO's report examines the firms telling big investors how to vote their shares. The findings pull back the curtain on the shareholder-meeting whisperers. The report asks who watches the advisers when they move billions with a recommendation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-865: Treasury's tech-buying board needed a tune-up in 2007 — GAO's report says its investment watch needed stronger operations and oversight. The findings target the money-behind-the-money: who guards the guardians of the tech budget. The report demands grown-up governance for the nation's fiscal computers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-165: GAO's 2007 report on Trade Adjustment Assistance — the aid that retrains workers whose jobs moved abroad — finds the training pot shallower than the Labor Department claimed. Once spent funds and firm pledges were both counted, states had less to work with. The report warns that rosy math could shortchange the very workers the aid was built for.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-265: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at health and Safety Information: EPA and OSHA Could Improve Their Processes for Preparing Communication Products. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-65: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at medicare Physician Payment: Care Coordination Programs Used in Demonstration Show Promise, but Wider Use of Payment Approach May Be Limited. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-665: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on defense Infrastructure: High-Level Leadership Needed to Help Communities Address Challenges Caused by DOD-Related Growth. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
hamlet-pg2265: The play within the play traps the King in this edition: "The play's the thing wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king." Hamlet watches Claudius blench at the poisoning. The mousetrap scene, the hinge of the greatest play.
hooke-micrographia-1665:
Robert Hooke published Micrographia in 1665 in London, the first major work of microscopy. Hooke, curator of experiments for the Royal Society, drew what the microscope showed him and printed the drawings as large fold-out plates. Readers saw a flea, a louse, and the edge of a razor as never before.

In the pores of cork Hooke saw tiny boxes, and he named them cells, a word biology still uses. He also studied crystals, plants, and insects, and guessed at the wave nature of light. The Royal Society backed the book, and Samuel Pepys sat up all night with it. Micrographia taught Europe to look closely.
i-secreti-de-la-signora-isabella-cortese: I secreti de la signora Isabella Cortese, 1565. The lady's secrets. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. History keeps its place secure. Readers can find it here.
jevons-coal-question-1865:
William Stanley Jevons published The Coal Question in 1865, asking whether Britain's prosperity could outlast its coal. Britain's factories, ships, and railways all ran on coal, and use was climbing steeply each year. Jevons, a young economist and logician, did the sums that few others had bothered to do.

He showed that coal use grew at a steady compound rate, so that even vast reserves would be strained within a few generations. He also noted a trap: more efficient engines did not save coal but spread its use, a pattern still called the Jevons paradox. Gladstone read the book and spoke of the national debt in its light. The work made Jevons famous overnight and stands as the first great study of resource limits, foreseeing the energy debates of a century later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lubeck-10165:
Lübeck, a free city of Germany on the River Trave near the Baltic Sea, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch. In 1900 the city counted 82,813 people, including 663 Jews. For centuries, the article shows, Lübeck tried to keep Jews out.

The account moves from a 1350 council letter blaming Jews for the plague to bans on overnight stays and the expulsion of 1699. Blocked settlers instead lived at nearby Moisling, under Danish rule, until French rule in 1811 ended the bans for a time. After the Congress of Vienna, the senate ordered Jews out again in 1816, and full emancipation came only with the law of October 9, 1848. A new synagogue followed in 1880. The entry is a record of exclusion, workaround, and slow legal change in one city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magino-meir-di-:
Meir di Gabriele Magino, a French silk manufacturer at Venice, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In 1587 he went to Rome to promote silk making there. That June he secured a sixty-year monopoly on silk manufacture by his improved process. Only the pope's sister shared in the profits.

The article notes the rare freedoms that came with his success. He was allowed to live outside the Roman ghetto for fifteen years. In 1588 he printed his Italian lectures on the uses and making of silk. He dedicated the book to Pope Sixtus V. The same year brought him a patent for polishing mirrors and cut glass with a vegetable oil he had discovered. The short entry records a Jewish craftsman whose skill bought him standing at the papal court itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mann-louis-1036:
Louis Mann, an American actor, receives a biographical entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in New York City in 1865, he was the son of Daniel and Caroline Mann. He began acting at six. In 1880 he toured with a small company.

The article follows his stage path through famous companies. He worked under the elder Salvini, Lewis Morrison, and J. K. Emmett in the 1880s. He then barnstormed in classical drama on his own. In 1887 he created Utterson the lawyer in a stage Jekyll and Hyde. Burlesque success came in 1896 with his Svengali turn in The Merry World. He then turned to German comedy parts, creating roles in a string of New York hits. In 1902 he took the lead in The Red Kloof. He later joined Weber and Fields until their partnership dissolved in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-masorah-10465:
The Masorah is the system of critical notes guarding the exact form of the biblical text. Crawford Howell Toy and Caspar Levias explain it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Generations of unnamed scholars built the system, the article says, from before the Maccabean age down to the year 1425. The name is disputed ground: taken from Ezekiel, it first meant a “fetter” binding interpretation, and only later came to suggest tradition handed down.

Readers learn where these notes live: some stand in separate works such as the Oklah we-Oklah. Others sit in the margins and end pages of handwritten Bible codices, and sometimes in the very lines. The article sets the Palestinian tradition apart from the Babylonian Masorah. Paul Kahle had lately brought the Babylonian terms to light. The article dates the Hebrew and Aramaic layers of the notes across a thousand years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-calw-calvo:
Meir Calw, also spelled Calvo, a biblical commentator, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn, and nearly everything about him is inference. The country and year of his birth are unknown. He quotes Levi ben Gershon, the great fourteenth-century philosopher-commentator, so the editors place him not earlier than the fifteenth century.

His one work is a commentary on the Pentateuch called "Minhah Hadashah," the New Offering. It never reached print as a whole: extracts from it were published by Heidenheim inside one of his editions of the Pentateuch, issued at Rödelheim between 1818 and 1821. For the rest, the entry rests on three standard bibliographies, Benjacob's, Steinschneider's, and Fürst's, which between them preserve this shadowy figure's name and book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendelssohn-106:
Mendelssohn is the German family made illustrious by the philosopher Moses and the composer Felix. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 treats the family collectively, in sections by six contributors. The line cannot be verified beyond the philosopher's father. Family tradition still claims descent from Moses Isserles. Abraham Mendelssohn comes first in the sample. He was the philosopher's second son and Felix's father. He was a Paris bank cashier and Hamburg partner, and a fugitive from the French siege in disguise. He co-founded the Berlin bank Mendelssohn and Co. He added Bartholdy to the family name.

Dorothea follows, the philosopher's eldest daughter, whose brilliance led her circle even in youth. Married unhappily to the banker Veit, she left him for Friedrich von Schlegel, was disowned, and followed Schlegel to Jena in 1799. The article proceeds member by member. It is a family biography of German Jewry's most famous house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyerbeer-giaco:
Giacomo Meyerbeer, born Jakob Liebmann Beer at Berlin on September 5, 1791, was the German composer who conquered the Paris opera stage. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He added Meyer to his name so his grandfather would leave him a fortune, and debuted as a pianist at seven.

After Italian successes, his Robert le Diable thrilled Paris in 1831, and Les Huguenots of 1836 came to be ranked even higher. Berlin's king made him general musical director, and Le Prophète circled the globe after 1849. He died in Paris in 1864 while rehearsing L'Africaine, a work he had nursed since 1838. The entry stresses that he held fast to Judaism and endowed fellowships for young musicians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minyan-10865:
Minyan, literally a count, is the quorum of ten men without which Jewish public worship cannot proceed. Cyrus Adler and Lewis N. Dembitz explain it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Boys over thirteen count as men. The ten, the writers suggest, survive from the oldest political arithmetic. Behind them stand Moses' chiefs of tens, Rome's decurio, and England's tithingman.

The Mishnah lists nine acts barred below ten. They include dividing over the Shema and passing before the Ark. They include lifting the hands in blessing and reading the Law and the Prophets. The mourners' and bridegrooms' benedictions are there, and God's name in grace after meals among them. The article then unpacks the references one by one. It is a legal minimum that shaped every small community's daily scramble to assemble ten.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-month-hebrew-ye:
The month — the stretch from one new moon to the next — is treated in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein, published in 1906. Genesis assigns the moon its office: to rule the night and serve for signs and seasons. In round numbers the biblical month ran thirty days, as the Flood narrative's hundred and fifty days for five months shows.

Twelve such months made a lunar year too short for the harvest festivals, so an extra month was slipped in from time to time to pull the calendar back to the sun. The article argues this correction is of the highest antiquity, since Passover and Tabernacles belong to fixed seasons of crops. After the Babylonian exile, it adds, the Jews took over the Babylonian month-names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-b-benjami:
Moses ben Benjamin ha-Sofer of Rome was a liturgical poet of the twelfth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give him a brief entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Almost nothing is recorded of his life beyond his city and his craft.

He wrote piyyutim, Hebrew liturgical poems, for Passover and for the Feast of Weeks. Others were written for some of the special Sabbaths of the year. The entry notes that his poems differ in style and build from those of the payyetanim before him. Even so short a notice helps map the Roman school of Hebrew poetry in the Middle Ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nadson-simon-ya:
Simon Yakovlevich Nadson was a Russian poet born at St. Petersburg on December 26, 1862. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His father was a Jew who had entered the Orthodox Church, and his mother was a poet of noble family. Nadson was commissioned an officer from the military academy.

In 1883 tuberculosis struck him, and he traveled abroad in search of health in vain. He died at Yalta on the last day of 1886, at only twenty-four. The entry says his death was hastened by persecution over his Jewish origin. His somber poems and essays were gathered in two volumes at St. Petersburg in 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-sir-matt:
Sir Matthew Nathan was an English soldier and colonial governor. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London on Jan. 3, 1862. He joined the Royal Engineers in 1880 from Woolwich. There he won the Pollock medal as top cadet.

Nathan served in Sierra Leone, Egypt, and India. He won a medal on the Lushai expedition of 1889. From 1895 he served the Colonial Defense Committee as secretary. He briefly ran Sierra Leone in 1899. In 1900 he became governor of the Gold Coast. It was a first such distant post for a Jew. Hong Kong followed in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuilly-sur-sei:
Neuilly-sur-Seine is a French town just outside Paris. Gotthard Deutsch and Simon Debré wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town's full population stood at 32,730. Its Jewish community was comparatively new in 1904. It then comprised about 250 families in all.

A small oratory in a hired hall came first, about 1860. After 1871 the congregation grew very fast. A consistorial decree organized the community in 1875. Its synagogue was dedicated on June 4, 1878. Rabbi Simon Debré's call, ten years later, brought prosperity. The community became one of France's largest in time. A refuge for homeless Jewish girls also stood there. Coralie Cahen had founded it back in 1866.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nittai-of-arbel:
Nittai of Arbela served the Sanhedrin as vice-president. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served under the nasi Joshua b. Peraḥyah. His day was that of John Hyrcanus. One source calls him Mattai of Arbela instead.

Arbela was a Galilean city near Tiberias. No legal rulings of Nittai survive at all. Three sharp sayings of his do survive. Shun an evil neighbor, he taught his hearers. Join not yourself unto the wicked, he added. Renounce not the hope of retribution, he closed. Hyrcanus had left the Pharisees for the Sadducees then. He was persecuting his former friends at that time. Nittai's words promised the sufferers he would be punished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oesterreichisch:
The Oesterreichisch-Israelitische Union was an Austrian group for Jewish rights. Gotthard Deutsch and Alexander Kisch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded in 1884, a year of loss. That year foes of the Jews won votes in Vienna. The group set out to guard Jewish needs in public life.

Its aims were plain and broad in scope. It sought to spread love for Jewish learning in Austria. It fought false claims and bias against Jews. It also fought moves to make such hate worse. Its board held men of law, trade, and the schools. Josef Bloch and Chief Rabbi Güdemann sat on it. Each winter it held free talks by known scholars. In 1895 it spurred a joint defense body for Austria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-origen-origenes:
Origen was a Christian thinker and teacher of the old church. Crawford Howell Toy wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Alexandria about the year 185. He died at Tyre about the year 254. His father trained him in study of the Bible.

Origen read deep thought with Ammonius Saccas, a sage. He gave his life to the study of faith through thought. He founded a school and swayed the church for years. His broad views drew a charge of false faith on him. His works gave rise to long fights in the church. Few of his many works have lived to our day. His notes on Matthew and John are chief among them. So is his reply to Celsus, a foe of the faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palermo-11865:
Palermo is the chief town of Sicily, an isle of Italy. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands on the north coast of that isle. Its Jewish group dates from the days of Rome. It is first named in the time of Gregory the Great.

By then the group held a synagogue and a hospital. A garden lay with that hospital for the sick folk. The bishop of Palermo seized both by force one day. He turned the synagogue into a church for his faith. The Jews, with aid from Rome, won a papal decree. It said the bishop must make full amends for the deed. The synagogue stayed a church, as it had been blessed. In 831 the Arabs took the town from Rome's rule. They treated the Jews of Palermo with justice, it says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peace-kiss-of-1:
The kiss of peace is a rite of the early Christian Church. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Joseph Jacobs wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The rite came just before mass or communion.

Paul's letters seem to point to the practice. Justin Martyr and Tertullian describe it in their writings. The article asks if the rite had Jewish roots. One scholar cited Philo on a kiss of harmony. Another found a kiss of peace for converts in Jewish texts. A third text shows God kissing the soul at death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pester-judische:
The Pester Jüdische Zeitung was a Hungarian Jewish newspaper. Herman Rosenthal and Ludwig Venetianer wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It came out five times a week in German. Oddly, it was printed in Hebrew type. Its readers were the Jews of Hungary.

I. Reiss founded the paper in 1869 at Pest. He had served as secretary to the chief rabbi there. The paper thrived during the Franco-Prussian War. It even printed a Hebrew map of the fighting. Reiss kept it clear of religious quarrels. After his death it continued under a new title.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pines-jehiel-mi:
Jehiel Michael Pines was a Russian Talmudist and Hebraist. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Rozhany in 1842. He traded as a merchant while teaching Talmud. His pen served the Hebrew press for decades.

In 1878 a London fund sent Pines to Jerusalem. He was to plant charities honoring Sir Moses Montefiore. He stayed in Palestine and worked for its colonies. Local rabbis banned him for meddling in affairs. Europe's rabbis backed him against the ban. He later directed Jerusalem's Ashkenazic hospital.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poniewicz-ponev:
Poniewicz is a district city in the government of Kovno, Russia. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1780 Count Nikolai Tyszkiewicz cut down a forest by the town. That work helped the city grow to its later size. Russia took the town after the last partition of Poland.

More than half the people of Poniewicz were Jews. A small Karaite group lived there too. In 1865 the town held 8,071 people, and 3,648 were Jews. By 1897 the total stood at 13,044. The town had one brick synagogue and seven of wood. The Karaites kept a synagogue of their own. Schools, a hospital, and a Talmud Torah served the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raab-hungarian-:
Raab, called Györ in Hungarian, is a chief town of its county. Gotthard Deutsch and Moritz Schwarz wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It holds one of the oldest Jewish groups in Hungary. In 1490 a Jew named Simon of Raab sued the town. By the sixteenth century its Jews had grown in count. Town records name a Jew street that faced the hill.

In the late seventeenth century war came to the town's Jews. A general's acts of those years fill the next part. The entry traces the group through tax, war, and return. It shows a small town where Jews lived from early times. Their street name alone keeps proof of that long stay.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ransohoff-josep:
Joseph Ransohoff was an American physician born on May 26, 1853. Cyrus Adler and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Cincinnati, Ohio. He earned his medical degree there in 1874.

The article follows his surgical study in five European cities. He returned home and taught anatomy from 1879 to 1902. He then took the chair of surgery at the same college. He also served on staff at Cincinnati Jewish hospitals. His papers treat the gall bladder, appendix, brain, and kidneys. The entry presents a surgeon known for both teaching and writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reines-moses-12:
Moses Reines was a Russian scholar born at Lida in 1870. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His father, Isaac Jacob Reines, was rabbi there. Moses died at Lida on March 7, 1891.

The article lists four works from his short life. Ruah ha-Zeman gathers material on Jewish culture in Russia. Nez̧ah Yisrael treats the Jewish people's survival. It also covers the settlement of Palestine. Aksanyut shel Torah studies the history of Russian yeshivot. Dor wa-Hakamaw gives lives of twelve modern scholars. He wrote all this before age twenty one. Two journal sources support the brief entry. Readers see promise cut short very early.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rindfleisch-127:
Rindfleisch was a German nobleman of Röttingen in Franconia. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He persecuted Jews in the thirteenth century. Civil war between two crown claimants set the scene.

The article tells how a host desecration charge spread from Röttingen. Rindfleisch claimed a heavenly mission to avenge it. He gathered a mob and burned Röttingen's Jews in 1298. His band then moved from town to town killing Jews. Only those accepting Christianity were spared, they say. Würzburg's large community was wiped out that July. Nuremberg's Jews fell after defending their fortress. Only Ratisbon and Augsburg escaped in Bavaria. About 120 communities were destroyed in six months. The entry records one of medieval Jewry's worst massacres.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-ferdi:
Ferdinand Rosenthal was a German rabbi born at Kenese, Hungary, on November 10, 1839. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He earned both a doctorate and his rabbinical title in 1866.

Rosenthal became rabbi at Beuthen, in Upper Silesia, in 1867. In 1887 he was called to Breslau, where he still served in 1905. His first book treated the First Book of Maccabees, in 1867. A later study weighed Caesar's decrees as Josephus reports them. His 1885 work covers four apocryphal books tied to Rabbi Akiba's school. He contributed steadily to the periodical press of his day as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabbath-schools:
Sabbath-schools, also called Sunday schools or religious schools, teach Jewish children their religion part-time. Joseph Jacobs and David Philipson wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Among Jews the form is a product of the nineteenth century.

Older communities ran the heder, a private day school for all instruction. There the child learned only Hebrew subjects: Bible, Mishnah, and Talmud. A split between secular and religious schooling came with the Mendelssohn era. Berlin's Freischule, founded in 1778, taught secular subjects beside the Hebrew ones. Like schools spread through Germany, then Europe, as Jews were emancipated.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schick-elijah-b:
Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Elijah ben Benjamin Schick. He was a Lithuanian rabbi and preacher. Schick was born at Vasilishok, in the government of Wilna, in 1809. He died at Kobrin on September 2, 1876. He studied under Benjamin, the chief rabbi of Grodno. As a rabbi he served in town after town.

Schick's posts included Diretchin, Lida, Novie Zhagory, and Kobrin. On Rosh ha-Shanah and Yom Kippur he also acted as cantor. His sermons always drew large crowds. He was known as one of the preachers people flocked to hear. His one book is 'En Eliyahu. It comments on Jacob Ḥabib's 'En Ya'aḳob, a classic gathering of Talmudic tales. The commentary was printed with the Wilna edition of that work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seal-13365:
Joseph Jacobs and Albert Wolf wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the seal. A seal makes an impression in wax or another soft substance. Jews used signets from a very early period. So did the other peoples of western Asia. The stones were cut in intaglio, often as cylinders or spheres. Seals attested documents in place of a signature.

Men guarded their seals as tokens of personal freedom. They wore them on a cord at the breast. Later they wore them on the right hand or on the arm. Many ancient Hebrew seals survive today. Telling them from Aramaic and Phoenician ones is hard. The scripts look alike, and the designs often match. The writing usually gives the owner's name. A father's or husband's name sometimes follows. A surprising number of the saved seals belonged to women.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbat-sabbath:
Shabbat is a treatise in the Mishnah, Tosefta, and both Talmuds. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The treatise deals chiefly with rules for keeping the Sabbath. It stands first in the Mishnah order called Mo'ed, on festivals.

Its twenty-four chapters hold 138 paragraphs in all. Early chapters cover carrying things between private and public ground. They also cover Friday tasks, lamplight, and Sabbath lamps. Bible passages on rest, from Exodus to Nehemiah, ground the rules. Readers get a map of the main rabbinic text on how Jews should spend the seventh day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silva-hezekiah-:
Hezekiah Silva was a Jewish author born at Leghorn, Italy, in 1659. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lazarus Grünhut wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. About 1679 he left home for Jerusalem in Palestine. There he studied at the yeshivah of Moses Galante.

Ten years later Jerusalem sent Silva to Europe for funds. At Amsterdam in 1691 he began printing his chief work. Peri Hadash comments on the Yoreh De'ah code of law. He stayed a year in that printing city. His free handling of legal problems drew a ban from Cairo's rabbis. That ban was later lifted by Abraham Levi. Silva died at Jerusalem in 1698. His son David edited two more parts of the work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-jos:
Solomon ben Joseph was a French liturgist of Avallon. Cyrus Adler and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He apparently lived in the thirteenth century there. He composed a number of liturgical poems, or piyyutim. One was a yozer written for the feast of Purim.

Another poem was a selihah on the massacre of Anjou in 1236. It gives the names of several martyrs of that attack. Two prayers of his use a striking formal device. Every line has four words starting with the same letter. Read downward, the first letters spell his name and the alphabet. The entry lists each of his surviving poems in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spira-spiro-139:
Spira, or Spiro, was a family of scholars and rabbis of Speyer. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, Meyer Kayserling, and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Branches spread across Germany, Bohemia, Galicia, and Poland. The family first bore the name Ashkenazi to mark itself apart.

Aaron Simeon Spira served as rabbi in many great cities. He led communities at Frankfort, Cracow, Vienna, and Prague. He lived an ascetic life and gathered many pupils. He wrote prayers on Prague's suffering under Swedish siege in 1648. Aryeh Löb Spira wrote on mathematics and Hebrew grammar as well. The long entry traces dozens of family members in order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strakosch-alexa:
Alexander Strakosch was a Hungarian actor and dramatic teacher born in 1845. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Sebes, near Eperies, on December 3. After a brief try at commerce he joined the stage. He first acted at Reichenberg in September 1863.

Strakosch danced, sang, and acted at Troppau and Hanover. In 1864 he went to Paris to study acting. There he gave readings from Schiller and Goethe. Heinrich Laube hired him as dramatic teacher in 1867. He taught at Leipsic and then at Vienna until 1879. Later he toured Europe as a dramatic reader. He spent one season in the United States. The entry follows a versatile stage teacher's career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taubes-aaron-mo:
Aaron Moses Taubes was a Rumanian rabbi and author. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and N. T. London wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He was born at Lemberg in 1787. In 1820 he became rabbi of Sniatyn and its districts. He died at Jassy in 1852.

In 1841 Taubes was appointed rabbi of Jassy. He stayed in that post until his death. His chief work holds responsa on the Shulhan Aruk. It answers questions across all four parts of the code. Some answers went to his son Samuel in letters. Others address his grandson Shalom Taubes directly. A second book holds his novellae on the Talmud. He corresponded with Solomon Kluger on legal questions. Jacob Ornstein, another famed rabbi, also exchanged letters. The entry honors a rabbi whose answers outlived him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tours-hebr-mord:
Tours, a French city on the Loire, had Jews from the sixth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Around 580 a Jewish tax-gatherer named Amantius was murdered there. His killers stripped him and threw him into a well. Later kings farmed out the Jews' revenues as gifts.

The Abbey of Saint Martin received that income in 1119. Jews owed the king set gifts at Easter and Christmas. Pepper, bread, wine, and meat made up the dues. Royal revenue from Tours' Jews soared by 1298. Expulsion came in 1306, and return in 1315. A poisoning charge drove them out again in 1321. Their quarter, la Juiverie, passed to the archbishop.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ukzin-stalks-of:
Ukzin, meaning stalks of plants, is the last treatise of the Mishnah. Sampson Lederhändler wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It treats ritual impurity passed through plant parts. Roots, stalks, and hulls form its main subject. Three chapters hold twenty-seven paragraphs in all.

Maimonides explains its closing place in the order. Stalk impurity rests on rabbinic judgment, not Scripture. Wet roots take impurity sooner than dry ones. A fig stalk counts with its fruit at egg size. Onion skins split into three classes of purity. Plants rooted in earth cannot become unclean at all. A famous later addition ends the Mishnah. It promises each righteous man 310 worlds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-venetianer-ludw:
Ludwig Venetianer was a Hungarian rabbi and writer. He was born at Kecskemet on May 19, 1867. Isidore Singer wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Venetianer studied at Budapest and at Breslau. He earned his doctorate in 1890. He received his rabbi's diploma two years later.

He served as rabbi at Somogy Csurgo, then at Lugos. In 1896 he moved to Ujpest, near Budapest. His books cover a wide range of topics. They treat charity in Jewish ethics and Hebrew Hungarian language study. He also wrote on how Jewish communities were organized in Europe. One work explains the ideas and teachings of Judaism itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-waley-simon-wal:
Simon Waley Waley was an English merchant, musician, and community worker. He was born in London on August 23, 1827. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was the younger brother of Jacob Waley. He studied at University College, London, but left without a degree.

At seventeen he wrote for the Times on trade. He later joined the stock exchange and its committee. For nearly twenty five years he ran the Jews' Free School office. Music filled the rest of his life. Moscheles and Sterndale Bennett taught him piano. He composed a concerto, trios, songs, and synagogue hymns. His hymns were sung for years in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wernikovski-jud:
Judah Wernikovski was a Russian Talmud teacher. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Slonim in 1823. He died at Jerusalem on February 20, 1901. As a child he was known as a Talmud prodigy. He married at age eleven.

Wernikovski studied at Volozhin's yeshibah and at Wilna. Ordained as a rabbi, he chose teaching instead. Men gathered in Slonim to study under him. In 1861 he became head of Slonim's yeshibah. He held that post for nearly forty years. His books treat Talmud tractates and collect his sermons. In 1900 he moved to the Holy Land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yarmuk-modern-s:
Yarmuk is a river of Palestine that flows into the Jordan. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its springs rise in the hills of Hauran and Jaulan. It runs west for most of its course to the sea.

It meets the Jordan four miles south of the lake. The river is thin and low for most of its length. At its mouth it is near as wide as the Jordan. There it runs thirty feet wide and five feet deep. A famed bridge of black stone spans it at that point. Rabbi Johanan called it the second river of the land. Its water could not serve for the rite of the red heifer. The entry rests on four books of tours and land lore.
kardec-le-ciel-et-l-enfer-1865:
Le Ciel et l'Enfer became the fourth book of Kardec's Spiritist canon in 1865. The Paris first edition is the text preserved here, in French. Kardec examines divine justice through the lens of Spiritism. Death, heaven, hell, and purgatory all come under review.

Spirit communications supply much of his evidence about the afterlife. He sorts the states of souls after death by their moral condition. Suffering, in his account, corrects rather than damns forever. An English version from 1878 survives only in libraries, with no free scan. The French original thus serves as the documentary edition. Spiritist readers rank it beside his other canon books.
king-arthurs-death-percy-1765:
King Arthur's Death is a traditional ballad fragment printed in Percy's Reliques of 1765. It is labeled a fragment here, as Percy found it, with its ending lost. The ballad sings of Camlann, Arthur's last battle against the traitor Mordred.

No Round Table pageantry fills these lines. Instead the verse is stark and bloody, king against false knight in a grim field. The folk singers kept the fall of Camelot brief and mournful. What survives reads like the memory of a disaster passed down by word of mouth. Percy's Reliques saved many such pieces, and this one shows the ballad at its most severe.
king-henry-vi-part-1-pg1765:
This early text of Shakespeare's Henry the Sixth, Part One comes from a 1592 file. Its makers warn readers that a better edition exists as Gutenberg number 100. The cast list prints the play's world plainly. King Henry's uncles and lords stand first, with Talbot and Fastolfe among the soldiers. King Charles of France, the Bastard of Orleans, and Burgundy make the French side.

Joan la Pucelle leads the French in the story, as Talbot leads the English. The play tells of England's war in France slipping away under a child king. It also plants the quarrels at home that grow into civil war. This old text preserves the play in a rough, early form, exactly as its printers left it.
kircher-mundus-subterraneus-1665:
Athanasius Kircher, the Jesuit whose learning seemed to cover everything, published Mundus Subterraneus in 1665. Twelve books map the world beneath our feet: volcanoes, quakes, caves, and a great central fire. Kircher drew on reports from travelers and his own descent toward a volcano's crater.

The Latin original is staged here as a documentary text, since no public-domain English version exists. Plates show dragons, giants' bones, and the earth's inner channels as Kircher imagined them. Wrong in many claims, the work still stands as the grand baroque picture of geology before the science had a name.
l-existence-de-la-pierre-merveilleuse-de:
A French work of 1765 argues that the philosophers' wonderful stone truly exists. A later note credits it most likely to Claude Chevalier and his wife. Chevalier was doctor to the Garde des Cent Suisses.

The book divides its case into clear parts. Six reasons argue that the stone is possible. Four classes of testimony aim to prove its truth. Sixteen opposing arguments follow, each with its own refutation. Its authors believed metal could truly change into gold. The neat division shows a lawyer-like wish to settle the question. Believers and skeptics both receive a full hearing on paper.
lecky-rationalism-1865:
W. E. H. Lecky published his history of rationalism in Europe in 1865. The full title traces the rise and influence of the spirit of rationalism. Lecky studies the decline of belief in magic, witchcraft, and miracles. He also treats persecution, skepticism, and the growth of science and industry.

His thesis is Whig history at its best: reason slowly defeats fear and dogma. Lecky marshals cases from trials, laws, and sermons across centuries. The book made his reputation while he was still young. Modern scholars nuance his story, yet its sweep impresses. It is a great Victorian argument for the power of free inquiry.
life-of-johnson-volume-1-1709-1765:
James Boswell's first volume covers Samuel Johnson from 1709 to 1765. George Birkbeck Hill edited this six-volume Oxford edition of 1887. Boswell promises Johnson's studies and works in chronological order. His correspondence and conversations with eminent persons fill the pages.

Original pieces by Johnson, never before published, appear here too. Boswell aimed to exhibit literature and literary men for half a century. Johnson's era in Britain unfolds through his daily talk. Volume One ends before Boswell's closest years with his subject begin. Johnson's unpublished original pieces appear here for the first time. The whole exhibits British literature across nearly fifty years.
lightfoot-galatians-1865:
Lightfoot's commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, in this 1896 edition, is the work that revolutionized English New Testament scholarship. Lightfoot treats the short letter as a doorway into Paul's whole world. Galatians, where Paul defends his gospel against rival teachers, rewards his close method.

He prints the Greek text with essays on the letter's date, its readers, and the history of the early church in Galatia. His notes weigh grammar, custom, and geography before drawing any doctrine from a verse. Students of Paul still learn the craft of commentary from Lightfoot's example. The commentary teaches by example how much a short letter can hold.
livingstone-zambesi-expedition-1865:
David Livingstone led a government expedition up the Zambesi from 1858 to 1864. His Narrative of an Expedition to the Zambesi and Its Tributaries appeared in 1865. His brother Charles and the geologist John Kirk were among the party.

The steam launch Ma Robert proved too weak for the river, and the Kebrabasa rapids blocked the way inland. Still, the party mapped the Shire highlands and reached Lake Nyasa, which Livingstone claimed for science. The Universities' Mission that followed met disaster, costing Bishop Mackenzie his life. Livingstone writes with honesty about failure, fevers, and the slave trade he saw growing.
lubbock-prehistoric-times-1865:
John Lubbock, a banker and neighbor of Darwin, published Pre-historic Times in 1865 and founded a discipline in the act. Lubbock coined the words Palaeolithic and Neolithic, the Old and New Stone Ages, which archaeology still uses. His book systematized the Stone Age from ancient remains.

He sorts stone tools, lake dwellings, and burial mounds into their ages, then turns to living peoples for light on ancient customs. The manners of modern peoples he called savages are read as survivals of the earliest human life. The method is dated and its language of its time. The framework lasted: this was the most cited prehistory of its generation.
marriage-of-sir-gawaine-percy-1765:
The Marriage of Sir Gawaine is a traditional ballad from Percy's Reliques, published in 1765. It tells the loathly lady story in plain sung verse. Folk singers kept this tale alive long after the courtly romances faded, and Percy printed it for a new age of readers.

To save King Arthur's life, Gawain agrees to marry a hideous hag. He treats her gently and grants her rule over herself in their marriage. At that gift, her ugliness lifts and she stands fair before him. The ballad is the folk root of the Ragnell romance. It states its moral plainly: courtesy and freedom work the change.
maxwell-dynamical-theory-electromagnetic:
James Clerk Maxwell, a Scots sage of the first rank, read this memoir on the field of electric force in 1865. He built it from the work of Faraday and from his own maths. Its aim was to join three fields that men had kept apart.

Maxwell's sums show that electric force, magnetism, and light are one thing in three forms. Light, in his scheme, is a wave in the same field that moves the compass needle. The claim set the tests that Michelson would try in the years to come, with strange results.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume six of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter thirty nine. Saint-Simon takes the waters at Forges for a tertian fever. News reaches him there of a fresh push by the princes of the blood.

At the King's communion, two dukes held the cloth with the chaplains. The princes sought the same honor without a duke called to aid. At the Assumption, M. le Duc served alone at the altar. Saint-Simon wrote at once to warn that no such thing had ever been done. He wrote to the Marechal and to M. d'Orleans on that breach. Rank at the altar was no small thing in that world.
new-system-of-physiognomony-sic-or-the-a:
M. Aguirre de Venero printed his New System of Physiognomony in New York in 1865, with John F. Trow as printer. The subtitle states the whole claim: the art of knowing men by their eyes. A verse from Luke heads the title page, about eyes being opened and men knowing Christ.

Physiognomy held that the face and body show the character within. Aguirre narrows that claim to the eyes as the key sign. Readers in 1865 bought many such guides to reading strangers at a glance. The book now serves as a neat record of that belief, stated in its boldest and simplest form.
openalex-w1574777265:
Jhon Rojas, Veronica Ochoa, and two co-authors ran this screening. It appeared in BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine in 2006. All four authors worked at the University of Antioquia. They tested ten plants used in Colombian folk medicine. Healers use those plants against infections, they note.

Farmers and healers collected the plants for the team. Ethanol, hexane, and water extracts were prepared from each. The team tested them against five bacteria and one yeast. Water extracts of three plants beat a standard drug on two bacteria. The sample reports those results from the abstract. Folk plants may aid treatment of common infections, they suggest.
openalex-w1752223565:
Xián Camanho, José Edelstein, Juan Maldacena, and Alexander Zhiboedov wrote this paper. It appeared in the Journal of High Energy Physics in 2016. The authors study corrections to how gravitons interact. Einstein's theory allows only one such basic structure. Wider theories permit extra structures beyond Einstein's form.

The team argues that causality limits those extra structures. A thought experiment with high energy scattering shows the risk. Breaking causality cannot be fixed with normal particles, they argue. It needs an endless tower of heavy, high-spin particles. For inflation, that means such particles should exist if signals deviate. The work links cosmic data to deep gravity rules.
openalex-w1990869665:
J. Allison and a large collaboration reviewed this simulation toolkit. Their paper appeared in the year 2016 in the catalog record. Geant4 simulates how particles pass through matter. Many experiments and projects rely on it worldwide. Uses span high energy physics, space science, and medicine.

It reports recent developments in the toolkit. Medical physics and radiation protection are among its fields. Astrophysics projects also model detectors with Geant4. Updates improve accuracy, speed, and range of materials. A shared, trusted toolkit keeps results comparable across labs. The review serves the huge community that builds on it.
openalex-w2080914865:
Teresa Coelho, Luis Maia, Ana Martins da Silva and colleagues studied long-term treatment for a rare nerve disease. Their paper appeared in Journal of Neurology in 2013. The disease runs in families and damages peripheral nerves. A faulty protein slowly harms nerves over years. The drug tafamidis stabilises that protein.

Patients from an earlier trial continued into this extension study. Some stayed on tafamidis, while others switched from placebo. Nerve scores stayed roughly stable in long-treated patients. Patients who switched later also slowed in decline. Early starters kept more nerve function overall. Side effects were similar between groups. No one stopped treatment because of side effects. Earlier treatment gave the greatest benefit.
openalex-w2091552865:
Miguel Angel Lanaspa, Laura Sanchez-Lozada, Christina Cicerchi and colleagues showed how uric acid speeds fructose harm in liver cells. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. Heavy fructose intake is tied to fatty liver. Effects vary greatly between people, though. The first step of fructose use involves an enzyme called fructokinase.

In human liver cells, uric acid raised fructokinase levels. More enzyme amplified fructose's fat-building effects. Blocking uric acid production largely stopped fat buildup. The effect worked in cells and in animals. A gene switch linked uric acid to the enzyme's rise. People prone to fructose harm often have high uric acid. It may be the hidden sensitising factor, they argue.
openalex-w2549670165:
Jean-Christophe Lagier, S. Khelaifia, and Maryam Tidjani Alou, with colleagues, published this letter in Nature Microbiology in 2016. The catalog record marks the article as retracted. It reports culturomics, a method that grows gut microbes under many culture conditions to identify them. DNA-only surveys had left many gut organisms unnamed and uncultured.

The team refined their culture recipes and applied them to human gut samples. They report identifying over a thousand prokaryote species, adding hundreds to the known gut repertoire. The additions included species never before isolated in humans and nearly two hundred possibly new ones. Genome sequencing was performed on the new species. Comparing culture with metagenomics, they claim culturing doubles the species isolated from the human gut. Readers should weigh these claims alongside the retraction marking.
openalex-w2784010265:
Åshild J. Vågene, Alexander Herbig, and Michael G. Campana, with colleagues, hunted an ancient epidemic's cause in this study, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution in 2018. After Europeans reached the Americas, introduced diseases killed huge numbers of indigenous people. The 1545 to 1550 epidemic in Mexico, called cocoliztli, was among the worst. Its culprit had been debated for over a century.

The team screened DNA from victims buried in an epidemic cemetery in Oaxaca using a metagenomic tool. They found Salmonella enterica, and rebuilt two genomes of its Paratyphi C variety. That bacterium causes enteric fever, a typhoid-like illness. The authors propose it contributed to the population collapse during the cocoliztli outbreak. The work shows ancient DNA can name pathogens behind historical epidemics. It turns a centuries-old mystery into a testable, evidence-based case.
openalex-w2904296365:
François M. Lutzoni, Michael D. Nowak, and Michael E. Alfaro lead a large team linking fungal and plant radiations in Nature Communications in 2018. Fungi eat by absorption; plants make food from light; their partnership is ancient. Interactions between them span mutualism, parasitism, and decay of dead matter. Success on both sides has often been credited to these relationships.

The paper evaluates whether fungi and plants diversified together in time. Interaction types sit unevenly across both family trees, the authors note. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi partner with about eighty percent of vascular plant families. Lichen-forming fungi make up a huge slice of one fungal subphylum. Such distributions hint at coevolutionary bursts rather than steady association. Testing timing turns natural history into evolutionary evidence. The study speaks to how symbiosis shapes the tree of life itself.
openalex-w3002058265:
Mark Khenkin, Eugene Katz, Antonio Abate, and colleagues issued this consensus statement in Nature Energy in 2020. It sets shared rules for testing and reporting how long perovskite solar cells last. Perovskites are a promising, cheap solar material, but they degrade in ways older solar products do not.

Studies of these devices had used inconsistent ageing tests, so results could not be compared and failure causes stayed hidden. The statement builds on the ISOS procedures, a standard set first agreed for organic solar cells in 2011. It adapts those procedures for perovskite devices. Common rules should let labs compare results directly and pin down what makes these cells fail.
openalex-w3004665465:
Noélie Bontemps, Pascal Lacroix, Éric Larose, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It watches a slow-moving landslide and asks what keeps it creeping. Most landslides are set off at once by moderate or large earthquakes, but this one moves in a different way.

The authors show that rain and small earthquakes together hold the slide in a persistent critical state, always near the point of moving. Quake shaking can raise stress on the sliding surface and weaken the soil by cracking the rock mass. Rain then changes water pressure underground, which can tip the balance days later. Tracking both forces explains the slide's slow, steady behavior.
openalex-w3022674365:
Reinhard Mechler, Chandni Singh, Kristie Ebi, and colleagues wrote this commentary in Sustainability Science in 2020. It examines Loss and Damage, the climate policy idea covering harms that adaptation can no longer prevent. Evidence now shows warming brings irreversible, even existential, impacts to exposed communities and countries.

The Loss and Damage debate has run for three decades and won a place in the Paris Agreement. Yet its scope and its relation to adaptation policy stayed vague. The authors review recent findings from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and other work. They draw out what the science means for future research and for policy that must face hard limits to adaptation.
openalex-w3200934665: A. Abada and a very large international collaboration produced this conceptual design report for a future hadron collider, called FCC-hh. It forms volume three of the Future Circular Collider design report. The report appeared in The European Physical Journal Special Topics in 2019. The preserved sample holds only the title pages and author list. It has no readable technical content, so the design itself cannot be described here.
openalex-w4206135665:
Peter Halfmann, Shun Iida, Kiyoko Iwatsuki-Horimoto, and colleagues tested the Omicron variant of the coronavirus in animals, in Nature in 2022. Omicron carries many mutations in its spike protein, the part the virus uses to enter cells. Those changes raised fears that vaccines and treatments might fail. Animal models let scientists test severity quickly and safely.

As the title states, Omicron caused weakened, or attenuated, disease in mice and hamsters. The finding mattered because earlier variants had caused severe lung disease in the same models. Milder illness in animals does not prove milder illness in people. Still, it gave early evidence that Omicron's biology differed from Delta's, and it shaped how risk was judged that winter.
openalex-w61562365:
Timothy Lynam, Wil de Jong, Douglas Sheil, and colleagues review tools for bringing community knowledge into natural resource decisions. Their review appeared in Ecology and Society in 2007. Local people hold knowledge and values that formal planning often misses.

The authors draw on long experience with forest communities. They first set criteria for judging participatory tools. They then describe each tool and weigh its strengths and weaknesses. They also judge how well each adapts to new contexts. Their findings suggest most tools are flexible enough to transfer. The review adds tips for avoiding common pitfalls. It remains a practical guide for managers who want community input to shape real decisions.
