openalex-w7131819265: This entry lists the contents of Volume 72, Supplement 1 (February 2026): papers from a medical meeting on 'Exercise is Medicine.' They cover exercise against frailty and muscle loss in aging, metabolic disorders, obesity-linked type 2 diabetes, muscle building with weights plus good nutrition, and even ties between exercise, diabetes, and Alzheimer's-related tau damage. Not one study but a whole meeting's worth of evidence that physical activity is itself medicine. Read it as a map of where exercise science stood in early 2026.
openalex-w7163924565: Imagine a memory that recalls different things depending on temperature. This theoretical paper builds a simple neural-network model that retrieves one pattern when hot and another when cold, by embedding each in a different network shape. The authors show temperature flipping the recall. Playful but rigorous work on memory with a thermostat.
openalex-w7204107965: Postpartum depression often starts before birth, making prenatal visits a chance to catch it early. This narrative review studies how screening during pregnancy affects detection and the baby's development. The authors trace the path from checkup to outcome. A maternal-health review arguing that asking early changes lives.
plos-pbio-0000065:
Yoav Soen, Daniel S. Chen, Daniel L. Kraft, and others reported a new lab method in PLOS Biology in 2003. Their tool uses tiny chip arrays of peptides held by MHC proteins. Those pairs are what T cells scan when they check whether a cell is healthy or infected.

Finding which T cells react to which peptide is slow work with older tools. A chip that tests many pairs at once can spot and sort reactive T cells far faster. That kind of map helps researchers track immune responses during infection or after a vaccine. It can also aid work on immune diseases, where the wrong T cells attack the body's own tissues.
plos-pbio-0020065:
Guang Yao, Mark Craven, Norman Drinkwater, and co-workers used yeast to map a toxic response pathway in PLOS Biology in 2004. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor is a vertebrate protein that reacts to dioxins and similar pollutants. It switches genes on and off, with effects that include harm to development.

Yeast lacks the receptor, which makes it a clean test bed. The team placed the pathway's parts into yeast and charted the contacts between them, step by step. That kind of map is hard to draw in animal cells, where many signals overlap. Their work lists the players in order and gives toxicology a clearer wiring diagram to test with new compounds.
plos-pbio-0020365:
Mikhail A. Lebedev, Adam Messinger, Jerald D. Kralik, and their team recorded from monkey prefrontal cortex in PLOS Biology in 2004. This front brain area handles planning and working memory. Monkeys did a task where the spot they attended and the spot they had to remember were sometimes different.

Nerve cells in the area coded both kinds of spots, letting the authors compare the two codes side by side. Knowing how attention and memory share or split cell resources is a basic question in brain science. The study gives hard data for models of how the front brain juggles what it sees now with what it must hold for later.
plos-pone-0000065:
Thomas Ruf, Teresa Valencak, Frieda Tataruch, and their team compared mammal running speeds in PLOS ONE in 2006. They found faster mammals tend to have more of a certain fat, called n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid, in their muscle membranes. The pattern held across species of very different sizes.

Cell membranes rich in these fats let pumps and signals work faster, which may support quicker muscle action. That would explain why speed tracks membrane makeup so well. The idea links diet and fat chemistry to peak performance in a broad way. It is a neat case of a small chemical trait scaling up to a whole-animal ability that anyone can watch.
plos-pone-0000165:
Juliet R. C. Pulliam, Jonathan G. Dushoff, Simon A. Levin, and colleagues published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines epidemic enhancement in populations where people are only partially immune. Enhancement means a disease can spread or sicken more, not less, when some immunity is already present.

Partial immunity is the norm for many real diseases, from dengue to flu. The authors model when it helps transmission instead of hindering it. Their results warn disease modelers that immunity cannot always be treated as a simple shield, a point with direct bearing on vaccine policy.
plos-pone-0000265:
Piers D. L. Howe and Margaret S. Livingstone published this vision paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Hermann grid illusion is a classic: stare at a grid of black squares and grey spots seem to appear at the crossings. The authors use the cancellation technique, adjusting a real stimulus to null out the illusion, to put a number on its strength.

Measuring an illusion precisely lets researchers test competing explanations of it. The cancellation method turns a subjective effect into a quantity. The paper gives vision science a firmer grip on one of its oldest puzzles, which probes how the retina and brain process contrast.
plos-pone-0000365:
Miguel Viveiros and co-authors examined in PLOS ONE in 2007 how the gut bacterium E. coli responds when antibiotics stress it. Their study links three things. It joins the pressure the drug puts on the cell and the genes the cell switches on in reply. It also tracks changes in how easily things pass through the cell's outer wall.

How permeable a bacterium's wall is can decide whether an antibiotic reaches its target inside. By tying gene responses to wall changes, the study addresses a core problem in drug resistance: bacteria that keep drugs out can survive treatment. The work fits the wider effort to understand how common bacteria adapt to the medicines used against them.
plos-pone-0000465:
Simon Melov and colleagues reported that exercise training rewound gene activity patterns of aging muscle, in PLOS ONE in 2007. As people age, skeletal muscle weakens and its gene expression shifts in characteristic ways. The team tested whether resistance exercise, weight training, could reverse that aging pattern in human skeletal muscle.

The title states their conclusion: resistance exercise reverses aging in human skeletal muscle, at least at the level of gene activity. That molecular evidence complements what trainers observe, that older adults regain strength with training. It also gives researchers measurable markers for testing other interventions meant to slow muscle aging.
plos-pone-0000565:
Nurit Kalderon and colleagues combined two strategies to treat spinal cord injury in an animal model, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The injury was an acute spinal cord contusion, a bruise like those from car crashes. Their therapeutic strategy paired cell elimination, removing harmful cells, with microsurgical intervention.

Spinal cord injury damages tissue twice: at impact, and again through inflammation and cell death in the hours after. A combined strategy addresses both waves. Studies like this test combinations because single treatments have repeatedly disappointed in this field, where even modest preserved function changes a patient's life.
plos-pone-0000665:
Kimberly A. Kelly, Jonathan Carson, Jason R. McCarthy and co-authors created a peptide tag for imaging inside living bodies, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Probes that label specific proteins have become critical for watching biological processes. The team used phage display, a screening method with viruses, to find a short peptide that binds near-infrared fluorochromes very tightly.

They call the peptide the IQ-tag. Near-infrared light passes through tissue better than visible light, so labels glowing in that range suit in vivo imaging. The title says the tag allows protein and cell specific labeling. A small, tight-binding tag can be attached to many targets, widening what doctors and researchers can see.
plos-pone-0000765:
Santanu Mukherjee, Mahmoud Abd-El-Latif, Michal Bronstein and colleagues studied how a small virus builds its shell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. SV40 is a small DNA virus without an envelope, wrapped in an icosahedral capsid 45 nanometers wide. The outer shell is composed of pentamers, five-unit clusters, of the major capsid protein VP1, linked by flexible arms at their tails.

Assembly builds the shell from those capsomers around the viral minichromosome. The title highlights high cooperativity: VP1 units do not assemble one by one independently, but promote each other's joining. Cooperative assembly explains how hundreds of proteins form one exact shell, a puzzle shared by many viruses.
plos-pone-0000865:
Shawna MacDonald, Gang Song and Chi-Sang Poon asked how breathing syncs with a ventilator, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Keeping a patient's breath in step with the machine is a major concern in intensive care. Lung volume feedback helps set the breathing rhythm, while steady pressure support can push against that rhythm if nothing balances it.

The authors focus on a simple form of learning, one that does not link two events together. They test whether this kind of learning helps the breathing system settle into the machine's pattern. The question matters for anyone designing ventilator care that works with the body rather than against it.
plos-pone-0000965:
Marybeth Langer, Lynn Sniderhan, Ueli Grossniklaus and colleagues described jumping genes leaving from an unusual site, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Transposable elements are DNA stretches that move around the genome and reshape it over time. Humans carry no active ones now, but our ancestors did, and their marks remain.

The team focus on excision, the cutting out step, happening at an atypical site. An odd exit point can create a new kind of element in the process. Cases like this show genomes are not fixed texts. They are edited by their own moving parts, sometimes in ways no one predicted.
plos-pone-0001065:
Hiroshi Akashi, Piyush Goel and Anoop John tested how well ancestral sequences can be inferred in fruit flies, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Reading the past state of a gene is critical to spotting the pattern and causes of molecular evolution. Among close relatives, that inference is usually assumed to be robust, but tests of the assumption were limited.

The team examine codon bias evolution in the Drosophila melanogaster subgroup. Codon bias is the uneven use of equivalent DNA spellings for the same building block. If ancestral calls are shaky, conclusions about bias may be too. Their check is methodological ground clearing for a busy field.
plos-pone-0001165:
Before a cell divides, a checkpoint makes sure every chromosome is properly attached to the spindle, the machine that pulls chromosomes apart. Théodora Niault, Khaled Hached, and Rocío Sotillo studied a checkpoint protein called Mad2 in female mouse meiosis, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Meiosis is the special division that makes eggs and sperm.

The authors changed Mad2 levels and watched chromosome segregation and checkpoint control in meiosis I. Too much Mad2 is known to hold cells in a prolonged arrest. Their work shows how sensitive egg formation is to the dose of a single checkpoint protein. That matters, because segregation errors cause miscarriage and birth defects.
plos-pone-0001265:
MicroRNAs, tiny regulators of gene activity, were still being discovered species by species in 2007. Thomas Sandmann and Stephen Cohen reported new ones for the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster in a PLOS ONE article that year. The full set of microRNAs was not known for any species, and many were believed to await discovery.

Working from the fly's recently assembled genome, the authors identified novel microRNAs and described how they found them. Each addition to the catalogue sharpens the picture of post-transcriptional regulation in development and disease. The fly, a workhorse of genetics, gains a fuller parts list.
plos-pone-0001365:
Rats communicate with ultrasonic calls that humans cannot hear. Markus Wöhr and Rainer Schwarting asked what one common call type means, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rats emit distinct types of ultrasonic vocalizations depending on age, state, and environment. The 50-kilohertz calls have been proposed as indices of a positive subjective state, a kind of animal contentment.

The authors tested whether playback of 50-kHz calls can induce approach behavior in listening rats. If the calls signal something good, listeners should move toward the sound. Their experiment speaks to how researchers read emotion in laboratory animals, where welfare and data quality both depend on it.
plos-pone-0001465:
Mahamadou Thera and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot tested in Mali. The shot targets a protein on the blood stage of the malaria parasite. The trial enrolled adults who face seasonal malaria in west Africa. It was a phase 1 trial, the first step, focused on safety.

Adults were split at random to get the shot or a control, with the dose raised in steps. The team tracked side effects and immune response in each group. A safe profile with a clear response would earn a trial in children. That is the group malaria hits hardest, so each step toward it counts.
plos-pone-0001565:
Mark Ungrin and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on growing human embryo stem cell clumps. Such clumps are the standard way to coax the cells to mature. But hand made clumps vary a lot in size and yield. That spread blurs tests and blocks scale up for care. The team built a way to form clumps in a uniform way.

Their method starts from single cells and yields clumps of set size at high rates. Uniform clumps give cleaner drug and growth tests. They also bring stem cell care closer to a true product. The work fixes a dull but real block in the field.
plos-pone-0001665:
Isabel Leroux-Roels, Roger Bernhard, Pascal Gérard, and their co-authors tested a bird flu vaccine in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The vaccine was built against clade 1 H5N1, one family of the bird flu virus. It was mixed with an adjuvant, an added ingredient that boosts immune responses. A vaccine stockpiled before a pandemic must also work against other families of the virus now spreading in birds.

The team checked whether the clade 1 vaccine raised cross-reactive immunity against clade 2 viruses. The full text gives the trial design, the antibody results, and how broad the protection looked. Broad cross-clade cover is a stated requirement for a pre-pandemic vaccine plan, so these results spoke directly to how health agencies should prepare.
plos-pone-0001765:
Anita M. Hennige and co-authors studied a liver protein tied to fatty liver and metabolic syndrome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Fetuin-A is secreted by the liver and rises in hepatic steatosis and metabolic syndrome. Those states come with low-grade inflammation and low levels of adiponectin, a protective fat-tissue hormone.

The team hypothesized fetuin-A helps drive both faults, and report that fetuin-A induces cytokine expression while suppressing adiponectin production. The full text gives the cell and tissue experiments. A single liver protein that fans inflammation and cuts a protective hormone is a plausible drug target. It sits in the cluster of disorders around type 2 diabetes.
plos-pone-0001865:
Bas B. van Rijn, Arie Franx, Eric A. P. Steegers, and their co-authors tested immune receptor genes in dangerous pregnancy disorders in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Altered maternal inflammatory responses play a role in preeclampsia and the HELLP syndrome, a severe variant involving hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. Both can kill mother and baby.

The team examined whether variants of the innate immune receptors TLR4 and NOD2, plus a pro-inflammatory phenotype, affect susceptibility to early-onset preeclampsia and HELLP. The full text gives the patient groups and the genetic results. Inherited inflammation settings could one day flag high-risk pregnancies early.
plos-pone-0001965:
Leah Owen and co-authors traced how a cancer-driving fusion protein mutes genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, EWS/FLI, is the master driver of Ewing sarcoma, a bone cancer of the young. Gene studies in a sarcoma cell line had shown the fusion switches more genes off than on. That makes it act in large part as a repressor.

The team followed one target, a gene switch called NKX2.2. As the title states, EWS/FLI represses genes through NKX2.2 during the shift to cancer. Naming the middleman gives drug work a new point of attack in a cancer with few options.
plos-pone-0002065:
Joseph Yu and co-authors followed HIV patients who moved clinics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Long-term retention on antiretroviral therapy in Africa's fast-growing programs was said to be sixty percent at two years. Yet many program reports said little about patients who transferred out to another facility, though Malawi's national figures showed transfers are common.

A patient counted as lost at one clinic may be in care at the next. The team asked what happens to those who transfer out. Fair counting matters: if transfers are thriving elsewhere, programs look worse than they are, and tracing efforts go to the wrong people.
plos-pone-0002165:
Albert Salehi, Sandra Meidute Abaraviciene, Javier Jimenez-Feltstrom, and co-authors studied faulty insulin release in diabetic rats, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In type 2 diabetes, the beta cells of the pancreas fail to answer rising blood sugar as they should, and in time they fail outright. The team suspected that too much nitric oxide made inside the pancreatic islets plays a part in that failure.

They used GK rats, a strain that develops type 2 diabetes on its own. In these animals, high islet nitric oxide went along with abnormal hormone release. A gut hormone, GLP-1, countered the effect, a clue for how GLP-1 based drugs may protect beta cells.
plos-pone-0002265:
Ivo Dinov, Daniel Rubin, William Lorensen, and co-authors presented a framework for organizing the tools of computational biology, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Progress in the field rests on three legs: new algorithms, systems to manage data resources, and tools that can work together. Without order, valuable resources sit scattered and hard to find.

iTools is a system for classifying, categorizing, and integrating computational biology resources in one registry. It gives researchers a single place to describe and locate tools and data. Shared registries of this kind keep a fast-growing field from drowning in its own output.
plos-pone-0002365:
Songkun Su, Fang Cai, Aung Si, and co-authors showed that Asian honeybees can read the dances of European honeybees, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The waggle dance lets foragers advertise the place of a food source to hive mates. It is famed as the only known form of symbolic communication in an invertebrate. Whether different honeybee species use the same code was an open question.

In mixed colonies, Asiatic honeybees understood the dance language of European honeybees and found the advertised food. The shared code hints that the dance dialects of bee species rest on a common, older system of spatial communication.
plos-pone-0002465:
Preisser and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Evan L. Preisser, Daniel I. Bolnick, among others. Its subject is the Many Faces of Fear: Comparing the Pathways and Impacts of Nonconsumptive Predator Effects on Prey Populations. Most ecological models assume that predator and prey populations interact solely through consumption: predators reduce prey densities by killing and consuming individual prey.

However, predators can also reduce prey densities by forcing prey to adopt costly defensive strategies. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002565:
Xu, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Dao-Zhen Xu, Kai Zhao, Li-Min Guo, among others. Its subject is a Randomized Controlled Phase IIb Trial of Antigen-Antibody Immunogenic Complex Therapeutic Vaccine in Chronic Hepatitis B Patients. The safety of the immune complexes composed of yeast-derived hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002665:
In 2008, Albert Nienhaus and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Interferon-Gamma release assay for the diagnosis of latent TB infection – analysis of discordant results, when compared to the tuberculin skin test. The catalog record names Albert Nienhaus first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. With the Interferon-γ release assays (IGRA) a new method for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis infections (LTBI) is available. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002765:
In 2008, Chanaz Salmi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about squalamine: an appropriate strategy against the emergence of multidrug resistant Gram-Negative bacteria?. Authorship is credited in the record to Chanaz Salmi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. We reported that squalamine is a membrane-active molecule that targets the membrane integrity as demonstrated by the ATP release and dye entry. A further point appears in the abstract. In this context, its activity may depend on the membrane lipid composition. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002865:
Jinze Xu and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of iron accumulation with age, oxidative stress and functional decline. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jinze Xu, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Identification of biological mediators in sarcopenia is pertinent to the development of targeted interventions to alleviate this condition. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002965:
Davendra Sohal, Andrew Yeatts, Kenny Ye and co-authors combined many microarray studies of blood stem cells in 2008. Microarrays measure gene activity across the genome, and vast data had built up across labs. Combining it is hampered by differing platforms and gene labels between studies.

Their meta-analysis found a novel signature, a shared gene pattern, for hematopoietic progenitor cells, the parents of blood cells. It also showed that data from different platforms can be integrated. Published in PLOS ONE, the paper is both a result and a proof that careful pooling of public data pays off.
plos-pone-0003065:
Qing-Bai She, Sarat Chandarlapaty, Qing Ye and co-authors studied breast tumor response to Akt signaling in a 2008 PLOS ONE article that was later retracted. Faulty PI3K/Akt signaling is common in breast cancers, arising from HER2 amplification, PI3K mutation, or PTEN loss. The objective was to test how Akt activation's role depends on which mechanism switched it on.

Readers should note the retraction status in the catalog title before citing any finding. The paper asked whether tumor cells with PI3K mutation or HER2 amplification depend selectively on Akt. Treat its claims as withdrawn unless independently confirmed elsewhere.
plos-pone-0003165: Hemant Kulkarni and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on judging AIDS risk in people infected with HIV-1. The title states its claim: a combined gene pattern, CCL3L1-CCR5 genotype, improves how well AIDS risk can be assessed. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record adds no data on methods or effect sizes.
plos-pone-0003265:
Deb K. Chatterjee, Kalavathy Sitaraman, Cassio Baptista and colleagues describe a protein array made on demand in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They describe a novel, simple and low-cost protein microarray strategy wherein arrays are generated by printing expression-ready plasmid DNAs onto slides. Those slides can be converted into protein arrays on demand, as the printed plasmids serve dual purposes.

Readers learn how storing DNA instead of protein can solve the fragility of protein chips. Proteins decay fast, while printed DNA keeps until needed. A cheaper, storable array could widen proteomics work beyond specialist centres.
plos-pone-0003365:
Mathieu Lihoreau, Cédric Zimmer and Colette Rivault test mutual mate choice in cockroaches in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Theoretical models of sexual selection predict both males and females of many species should benefit by selecting their mating partners. However, empirical evidence testing and validating this prediction is scarce. In particular, inbreeding avoidance is expected to influence choice by both sexes.

The title states when it pays both sexes to avoid inbreeding, under mutual mate choice. Readers get a rare two-sided test, since most mate choice studies examine females alone. Avoiding inbreeding is a benefit clear enough for both sexes to act on.
plos-pone-0003465:
Abdiaziz S. Mohamood and co-authors studied how the immune system prunes T cells in this 2008 paper. A pathway called Fas orders extra or faulty T cells to die. Which T cell groups that pathway controls in the body was poorly defined. Most mature T cells carry either CD4 or CD8 markers.

The team found Fas constantly purging one odd group, double negative T cells. Removing those cells shapes the mix of the wider T cell pool. Steady pruning keeps the immune repertoire in balance. It may also guard against attacks on the body's own tissues.
plos-pone-0003565:
Lia E. Perez and co-authors studied a brake on platelet-making cells in this 2008 paper. A phosphatase called SHIP-1 dials down signals from cytokine receptors. Those signals help drive megakaryocytopoiesis, the making of platelet parent cells. Thrombopoietin is one of the key signals involved.

The authors tested whether SHIP-1 controls early megakaryocyte progenitors. It negatively influenced those early cells in their assays. A brake at that stage sets later platelet output. Disorders of too many or too few platelets may involve this control. Platelet counts must stay in a tight range to keep blood clotting safe.
plos-pone-0003665:
Tjeerd G. Kimman, Sander Banus, Naomi Reijmerink, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Protection after whooping cough vaccination differs from child to child. The team studied genes in the Toll-like receptor pathway, a set of sensors that help start immune responses.

They linked combinations of these genes to the strength of the antibody response after pertussis vaccination. Single genes alone did not tell the story; interacting genes did. The work suggests vaccine response is a property of the immune wiring as a whole, not of one part.
plos-pone-0003765:
Tong Zhou, Peter J. Enyeart, and Claus O. Wilke published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. When selection favors a protein's new function, mutations can pile up in a small stretch of DNA. Such clusters are fingerprints of adaptation. An earlier method for finding them had a flaw involving solvent exposure.

The authors present an improved way to detect clusters of mutations. Their approach accounts for how buried or exposed each site in a protein is. It separates the marks of positive selection from random noise more cleanly than the method it revises.
plos-pone-0003865:
Travis I. Moore, Ching-Shan Chou, Qing Nie, and colleagues published this yeast study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Moving or growing up a chemical gradient is a universal behavior of living things. Baker's yeast cells do it when they follow the mating pheromone alpha-factor toward a partner.

The team tested yeast a-cells in a microfluidics chamber that held a steady pheromone gradient. The cells sensed the gradient across their own tiny surface and responded robustly. The work shows single cells navigating by smell with precision, despite noise in the signal.
plos-pone-0003965:
Stéphane Hausmann, Jean-Baptiste Marq, Caroline Tapparel, and co-authors studied a virus sensor in cells in 2008. Most RNA viruses start copying with building blocks that leave tagged RNA ends. Cells use a sensor called RIG-I to spot such RNA. That spotting switches on interferon-beta, an antiviral alarm.

Their PLOS ONE article examines how double-stranded RNA triggers that alarm. Many viruses depend on RIG-I detection to be noticed at all, they note. Pinning down the trigger sharpens models of early immune defense. It also informs design of vaccines that use RNA signals. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004065:
Jérôme Sueur, Sandrine Pavoine, Olivier Hamerlynck, and co-authors proposed listening as a biodiversity survey tool in 2008. Counting species is among the hardest tasks in conservation work. Habitat loss keeps raising the urgency of fast assessments. Sound offers a shortcut where many animals call.

Their PLOS ONE article tests a rapid acoustic survey for appraisal. Recorded soundscapes can index how rich a site is. The approach covers large areas faster than trapping or transects. It will not name every species, but it ranks sites for protection. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004165:
Hans-Martin Herz and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In yeast, a set of genes builds the ESCRT complexes, sorting machines that route proteins at the early endosome, a cell's sorting station. In the fruit fly, faults in one ESCRT-II part, vps25, cause sorting defects, a build-up of Notch protein, and excess Notch signalling.

The team compared the fly's ESCRT-II components, looking for what they share and where they differ. Their genetic tests separate common duties from unique ones within the complex. The results clarify how this sorting machinery controls signals that guide growth and development.
plos-pone-0004365:
Gabriele Hörmannsperger and colleagues published this probiotic study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The probiotic mixture VSL#3 is a blend of live bacteria used for gut health. Clinical and lab studies suggest it protects patients in inflammatory bowel disease, a long-term inflammation of the gut. How its bacteria calm that inflammation, strain by strain, was not clear.

The team worked with intestinal epithelial cells, the cells lining the gut. They tracked IP-10, a chemokine that calls immune cells to a site. They report that the bacteria block IP-10 release after the protein is made, a post-translational effect. That is one way friendly bacteria can calm an inflamed gut.
plos-pone-0004465:
Knowing your left from your right feels fixed, yet Eve Dupierrix, Michael Gresty, Theophile Ohlmann, and co-authors show it can drift for a long time, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Our sense of the body's main directions, right-left, up-down, ahead-behind, seems absolute. In fact it can be reshaped by what the senses and muscles experience.

Earlier work showed that long exposure to distorted spatial cues can tilt this inner compass. Here, the team found that normal sense-and-motion interaction alone can induce lasting egocentric disorientation, a loss of bearings centered on one's own body. Volunteers came away unsure of directions they normally never question. The finding matters for pilots, divers, and patients whose balance systems mislead them.
plos-pone-0004565:
Multiple sclerosis may follow a chain of causes spread across a lifetime, proposes Douglas Goodin in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease, in which the immune system attacks the insulation of nerves, seems to involve both genetic susceptibility and environmental risk factors. Goodin sets out a model he calls the causal cascade.

In the model, three environmental factors act in sequence. The first acts near birth, the second during childhood, and the third long afterward. Two candidate factors are examined against this scheme. A staged model like this explains why the disease starts in early adulthood yet may be seeded in infancy. It also tells researchers where to look: different causes at different ages, each testable.
plos-pone-0004665:
Gene patterns in Mediterranean fruit flies from Argentina inform a pest control method that breeds its own downfall, report Alicia Basso, Laura Martinez, and Fanny Manso in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Mediterranean fruit fly, Ceratitis capitata, is a major agricultural pest in Argentina. Control programs based on genetic strategies, such as releasing sterile males, are non-contaminant: they leave no poison in the field.

Success of those programs depends on compatibility between natural and laboratory fly populations. The team studied genetic polymorphisms within and between founder populations of the fly. If lab flies differ too much from wild ones, released males will not mate and the program fails. Population genetics, in this case, is applied pest control.
plos-pone-0004765:
Morihiro Higashi and colleagues showed that human Mena protein partners with Rac1 in brain tumor cell lines, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mena helps cells move by shaping the actin scaffold that pushes the cell edge forward. Rac1 is a switch protein from the Rho family that also drives edge protrusion and cell motion.

The team tested whether the two proteins interact in glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor. They found Mena does associate with Rac1 in those cell lines. Paired control of actin may drive tumor cell invasion. That pairing could be a drug target. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004865:
Shinichi Sunagawa and colleagues found a taxonomically restricted cysteine rich protein family in reef building corals, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genomic sequence information grows exponentially while identification of genes without known homologs remains a major challenge. For non model organisms with limited resources. High throughput transcript data offer a route to characterize novel families such as small secreted proteins in stony corals.

Coral specific proteins may underpin skeleton building. Reef resilience could depend on such novelties. Cataloguing them aids conservation genomics. Corals face bleaching and acidification threats. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0004965:
Working memory holds information for a few seconds. For smells, its machinery was unknown. Christina Zelano and colleagues addressed that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked whether odor memory uses a verbal representation. They also asked whether it uses a sensory image of the odor itself. Brain scanning helped locate the substrates of each.

Volunteers performed odor memory tasks during scanning. The primary olfactory cortex held the odor trace. Word areas were not the main store. The brain keeps a dedicated buffer for smells in the smell cortex itself. The finding maps a small but distinct corner of human memory.
plos-pone-0005065:
Inside one patient, HIV keeps changing. It swaps gene pieces with itself, creating hybrid viruses. Susanna Lamers and colleagues measured that mixing in PLOS ONE in 2009. They analyzed 780 viral sequences from 53 tissues. The samples came from patients after death. Infected macrophages are tied to tissue damage and viral persistence.

Recombination was extensive, and it was common in tissues with abnormal histopathology. The mixing runs hottest where tissue is sickest. It may help the virus persist in damaged organs. The work shows HIV's shape-shifting has a geography. Understanding that geography matters for cure research. Reservoirs hiding in diseased tissue may be the hardest to clear.
plos-pone-0005165:
The RTS,S malaria vaccine was a landmark candidate. It protected Mozambican children for at least twenty-one months in trials. Caterina Guinovart and colleagues dug into that protection in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their paper reports further results from the phase IIb trial. Protection varied between endpoints, like parasites in blood versus clinical malaria.

The follow-up explored why protection lasted. It examined the mechanisms behind the vaccine's effects. Understanding durability guides the next generation of malaria shots. A vaccine that fades fast needs boosters or redesign. This analysis helps decide which. It also shows children's immune responses in detail. Malaria still kills many children yearly. Every insight into lasting protection counts.
plos-pone-0005265:
The hippocampus is a brain region central to memory, and its size is often measured in brain studies. Tracing it by hand is the trusted method, but it is slow and prone to error. Cherbuin and colleagues compared hand tracing with automated methods in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The comparison used a large community-based sample and linked the measures to memory performance. Automated segmentation would allow far bigger studies if it matches hand tracing well. The head-to-head test tells researchers when the fast method can be trusted. Large scans of the aging brain depend on fast methods, and this head-to-head test tells labs when the fast road is safe to take and when it is not.
plos-pone-0005365:
The tree Ailanthus excelsa, a relative of the tree of heaven, has a root bark used in traditional remedies. Lavhale and colleagues isolated a new compound from that bark, named AECHL-1, and reported it in PLOS ONE in 2009.

AECHL-1 is a triterpenoid, a class of plant compounds often active against cancer cells. The compound showed anti-cancer activity against a variety of cancer cell types in their tests. A new molecule from a known medicinal tree gives drug hunters a fresh starting structure. Plant drugs have a long past in cancer care, from yew bark to the Madagascar periwinkle. So a new bark compound joins a line that has paid off more than once in the past.
plos-pone-0005465:
Caren Smith and colleagues studied a gene, blood fats, and memory in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The gene APOC3 helps control how the body handles fats in the blood, and insulin in turn controls the gene. Poor fat profiles in blood are linked to heart and brain problems.

The team studied Hispanic adults with roots in the Caribbean and checked gene forms, diabetes, and thinking scores. They looked for links between the gene and both sugar control and mental performance. Such links could show one path by which diabetes and blood fats affect the aging brain.
plos-pone-0005565:
Juan Carlos Montero and co-authors studied a growth enzyme in early breast cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, and some patients relapse even after treatment improves. Better markers are needed to tell which cancers will return.

The team measured an enzyme called Erk5 in early-stage tumours and tracked how patients fared. Tumours with more of the enzyme were linked to shorter disease-free times. That link makes Erk5 both a warning marker and a possible target for new drugs. A marker measured in the first tumour could help sort patients into closer or lighter follow-up.
plos-pone-0005665:
Mehdi Namdar and co-authors tested caffeine's effect on heart blood flow in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Caffeine is one of the most widely used active substances in the world, in coffee, tea, and medicines. Its short-term effect on blood flow in the heart muscle was largely unknown.

The team gave patients with coronary artery disease, and matched healthy controls, a dose equal to about two cups of coffee. They then measured how the heart's blood flow answered exercise. Caffeine blunted that answer in both groups, a result patients may want to know before stress tests.
plos-pone-0005765:
Masamichi Koyanagi and co-authors showed in 2009 that a Wnt signal boosts heart gene activity in human blood-borne progenitor cells. These circulating cells can help repair tissue, and Wnt signals steer whether stem cells multiply or mature. Earlier work hinted non-canonical Wnts push them toward heart fates.

The team found Wnt5a raises cardiac gene expression through a PKC delta route. More heart-ready cells could aid repair after a heart attack, a leading killer. The study maps one step of that steering in human cells, not just animals. Such steps are what cell therapy must master before clinic use.
plos-pone-0005865:
Christina Sehlmeyer and co-authors reviewed in 2009 what brain imaging has shown about human fear learning and its undoing. Fear conditioning pairs a neutral cue with something aversive; extinction then teaches that the cue is safe again. Both processes mirror what goes wrong, and right, in anxiety disorders.

The systematic review gathered neuroimaging studies of conditioning and extinction in people. Common circuits emerged, centered on the amygdala and prefrontal areas. Knowing the normal circuitry sharpens the search for faulty patterns in phobias and PTSD. It also helps judge therapies, like exposure, that work through extinction.
plos-pone-0005965:
A vaccine that guards against pneumococcal disease can also shift which strains cause trouble. Tom Karnezis, Ann Smith, Susan Whittier and colleagues tracked that shift in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study follows drug resistance among bacteria causing invasive pneumococcal disease, before and after the PCV-7 vaccine came into use in the United States.

Trends of this kind have differed from place to place, so local records matter. If resistant strains grow more common after a vaccine arrives, treatment guides must change with them. The study gives doctors and health planners a grounded picture of one vaccine's side effects on resistance, drawn from real cases of severe disease.
plos-pone-0006065:
Rivalry can make a bacterium better at eating. Hiren Joshi, Rachna Dave and Vayalam Venugopalan showed that twist in Pseudomonas putida in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies how competition between species triggers a plasmid, a small ring of extra DNA, to boost the range of foods the bacterium can use.

Plasmids are shared between bacteria, so a boost can spread through a community. Competition, usually read as a force that narrows niches, here widens one. The finding helps explain how diverse microbe communities hold together, and it shows a mobile gene at work as a rapid answer to a crowded world.
plos-pone-0006165:
A mouthwash rinse might carry enough DNA for a genome study. Tetyana Zayats, Terri Young, David Mackey and colleagues graded that DNA in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper assesses the quality of DNA extracted from mouthwashes, a cheap, safe source of buccal cells that can be collected by mail without a clinic visit.

Large genetic studies stand or fall on cheap, easy sampling, so a mail-in rinse is attractive. Yet its quality had drawn little attention before this check. Knowing how mouthwash DNA performs, and where it falls short, tells study designers whether the savings are real or a false economy paid for in failed samples.
plos-pone-0006265:
Malignant catarrhal fever kills cattle with vessel inflammation, tissue death, and runaway immune cells. Claudia Meier-Trummer and colleagues linked the disease to a sheep herpesvirus, OvHV-2, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The virus is thought to trigger the illness even though sheep carry it without harm.

Diseased cattle showed low levels of the IL-2 transcript, an immune signal, in their samples. Most viral genes stayed in a latent, quiet profile rather than active copying. A mostly sleeping virus causing severe disease is a puzzle the data sharpen. The profile may explain why the immune response misfires so badly.
plos-pone-0006365:
Pandemic plans rely on local health workers actually reporting for duty. Daniel Barnett and colleagues surveyed that willingness in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on pandemic influenza. Local agencies play a central role in response, making staff willingness a critical planning concern.

The survey applied the Extended Parallel Process Model, which weighs perceived threat against coping confidence. Workers who feel able to act are more likely to show up. Planners can raise willingness by addressing fears and barriers in advance. The findings turn an assumption of preparedness into measured evidence. Plans built on real survey data stand a better chance of working when a crisis hits.
plos-pone-0006465:
Mark Polhemus and colleagues tested malaria vaccine candidates in adults for PLOS ONE in 2009. The trial took place in an area with high malaria transmission. Its main aim was to compare the safety and reactogenicity, the short-term reactions, of two versions of the RTS,S vaccine. One version, with the AS01B adjuvant, was newer; the other, with AS02A, had been studied more widely.

The trial was a phase IIb, single-center study in adults. It advanced the newer candidate toward use in populations where malaria is endemic. Safety data in exposed adults is a key step before wider trials. Malaria still kills many people, so each step in vaccine testing counts.
plos-pone-0006565:
Peter Chen and co-authors studied how injured lungs heal in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lung injury turns up an enzyme called MMP7. This enzyme is needed to call in white cells and to regrow the surface cells of the lung. MMP7 does part of that job by shedding syndecan-1, a protein that sits on the cell surface and is cut loose.

Their title says this shedding helps regrowth by changing the grip of cells through integrin proteins. Cells must loosen and grip again as they crawl to close a wound. The shedding and the grip change work as one plan. Knowing the plan may guide new care for severe lung injury.
plos-pone-0006665:
Xiaohui Wang, Yujun Song, Jinsong Ren, and colleagues silenced a cell cycle protein in leukemia cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cyclin A2 is critical for initiation of DNA replication, transcription, and cell cycle regulation. Cumulative evidence indicates deregulation of cyclin A2 is tied to tumor development. The team knocked down cyclin A2 by siRNA in K562 leukemia cells upon certain treatments.

Their title reports knocking down cyclin A2 suppresses apoptosis and switches differentiation pathways. The result is double-edged: less death but more differentiation. Differentiation therapy is a real strategy in leukemia. Knowing a cyclin's role refines that strategy.
plos-pone-0006765:
Nina S. N. Lam and colleagues surveyed New Orleans businesses deciding whether to return after Hurricane Katrina in PLOS ONE in 2009. Katrina struck the city on August 29, 2005. It ranks among the greatest American catastrophes. Hard data on how businesses respond afterward are rare. The team analyzed repeated telephone surveys of local businesses.

Surveys ran from December onward as owners weighed returning. Owners faced deep uncertainty about customers, workers, and repairs. Tracking decisions over time shows what tipped them toward returning. Loyalty, damage, and expectations all played roles. The evidence can guide recovery policy after future disasters. It shows recovery as a chain of business decisions, not just rebuilding.
plos-pone-0006865:
Jessica M. Bon and colleagues related blood markers to scan patterns and smoking in lung disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease mixes airway remodeling with tissue destruction. Some patients are airway-dominant and others parenchyma-dominant. Unique biomarker patterns for each type would support distinct phenotypes. The team tested blood biomarkers against radiographic patterns.

Smoking status also influenced the biomarker patterns. Separating disease types by blood test could guide personal treatment. Imaging is expensive, so a blood pattern is attractive. The results strengthen the case that COPD is several diseases in one label.
plos-pone-0006965:
Lyle McKinnon, Xiaojuan Mao, Joshua Kimani, and colleagues mapped immune targets in HIV in PLOS ONE in 2009. Killer CD8 T cells are a main defense against HIV. Many vaccine plans aim to raise these cells. The exact viral pieces they attack can differ between populations. The team studied a group where clade A1 infection dominated.

They mapped the epitopes, the viral fragments these T cells recognize. Knowing the targets in this population is practical knowledge. A vaccine built for one region may miss the marks elsewhere. Their catalog helps match vaccine design to the viruses people actually carry.
plos-pone-0007065:
Jorge Goldstein, Winston Morris, César Loidl, and colleagues studied a bacterial toxin in rodents in PLOS ONE in 2009. Epsilon toxin comes from Clostridium perfringens types B and D. It causes enterotoxaemia, a deadly disease of sheep and goats. In stricken animals it damages vessel linings, causing swelling in lungs and brain.

The team tested the toxin's effect on the small intestine of mice and rats. Intestinal permeability rose after exposure. A leakier gut may be an early step in the poisoning. Understanding that step could help protect livestock from a fast and often fatal disease.
plos-pone-0007165:
Yufeng Tong, Wolfram Tempel, Lyudmila Nedyalkova, and colleagues solved an enzyme's structure in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme GNE runs a key step in making sialic acid. Faults in it cause a rare urine disorder or a muscle disease called inclusion body myopathy. GNE is the only human protein holding a certain kinase domain type.

The team crystallized the N-acetylmannosamine kinase domain of GNE. Its structure shows where disease mutations fall and how the enzyme grips its substrate. That map helps explain the muscle disease at atomic level. It may also guide efforts to stabilize the faulty enzyme.
plos-pone-0007265:
Ji-Hyun Lee, Michael J. Schell, and Richard Roetzheim addressed statistics for group randomized trials in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. These trials randomize whole groups rather than individuals. They are common in health promotion and disease prevention programs, where treating one person alone is impractical or would contaminate the study.

Responses are still measured on individuals inside each group. Problems arise with multiple binary endpoints and only a small number of groups. The authors present analysis methods for that setting. Their guidance helps researchers avoid false conclusions when community-level trials produce several yes-or-no outcomes.
plos-pone-0007365:
Luuk Gras, Suzanne Jurriaans, Margreet Bakker, and colleagues tracked changes in HIV levels in the Netherlands in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. HIV RNA levels at viral set-point predict disease outcome. Set-point is the stable virus level reached after early infection, and it also shapes transmission dynamics of HIV in populations over time.

The authors ask whether set-point levels changed over the last decade of the epidemic. They investigate plasma HIV RNA and CD4 cell counts over time. They report set-point viral load levels have risen. Rising set-points could mean faster disease and easier transmission.
plos-pone-0007465:
Yuji Yasukochi and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 comparing the chromosomes of two moths: the tobacco hornworm and the silkworm. The silkworm genome is well studied, but most other insects lack such resources. A technique using glowing DNA probes, called BAC-FISH, lets researchers map genes directly onto chromosomes. The team used it to align the two species' karyotypes.

The maps revealed extensive conserved synteny. Long stretches of genes sit in the same order in both moths despite their long separation. That conservation is a practical gift to insect science. Knowledge gained in the silkworm can be transferred to relatives with far less work. The study also gives a picture of how slowly moth chromosomes have rearranged over evolutionary time.
plos-pone-0007565:
Jon Kuchenreuther and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was hydrogenases, enzymes that work with hydrogen gas where no oxygen is present. The iron-based kind carry a rare metal core at their heart. Building that core takes help from several other enzymes. Working outside living cells, the team searched for small compounds that speed up the enzyme's start-up in a test system.

Three plain compounds did the job: two amino acids, tyrosine and cysteine, plus a common cell chemical known as SAM. Together they boost the start-up of the hydrogenase in the dish. A good recipe for waking the enzyme outside cells is a real help. It lets researchers study clean hydrogen output under set conditions. Such enzymes draw interest from green-fuel work, since they make hydrogen with no waste. Small compounds that switch them on are handy tools.
plos-pone-0007665:
Joseph Abrajano and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the brain's support cells get their identities. REST is a master regulator that silences neuronal genes outside neurons. It works with partners, including CoREST, at many sites in the genome. The team studied how REST and CoREST are deployed during the making of glia, the brain's support cells. Their focus included oligodendrocytes, the cells that wrap neurons in myelin.

REST and CoREST are used in different patterns across glial subtypes. That differential deployment promotes subtype specification and the maturation of the oligodendrocyte lineage. Two related silencers, scheduled differently, produce different cell fates. Myelin-making cells matter in diseases where insulation fails. Understanding their maturation program is a step toward repairing it. The study maps a control layer of brain development that works by repression.
plos-pone-0007765:
Liang Li and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It searches the genome for markers that predict response to two cancer drugs. The drugs are gemcitabine and AraC, both copies of a DNA building block. Patients vary widely in how they respond to chemotherapy.

The team ran a genome-wide association study using cell line data. They linked DNA variants to how strongly the drugs worked. Such markers are called pharmacogenomic biomarkers. If they hold up in patients, doctors could test DNA before choosing a dose. That promises stronger effects with fewer side effects.
plos-pone-0007865:
Rogier Thurlings and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tracks immune cells moving into inflamed joints in rheumatoid arthritis. In this disease, macrophages drive the inflammation of the joint lining. Studies from the 1960s suggested those macrophages are steadily replaced by monocytes from the blood.

The team used monocyte scintigraphy, a scan that follows labeled monocytes in patients. Imaging shows the dynamics of that migration in living people. If fresh monocytes keep refueling the joint, blocking their entry could calm disease. The scan itself may become a way to measure treatment response.
plos-pone-0007965:
Debbie Liao and colleagues showed how a tumor's neighbor cells help it spread, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fibroblasts are support cells, and those tied to cancer are often the tumor's most common neighbor. The team used a mouse model of breast cancer known as 4T1.

The support cells did not just sit by. They reshaped the immune scene around the tumor in ways that fed growth and spread to new sites. That makes them a target in their own right. A drug that calms these helpers might slow the cancer. It would not need to aim at the tumor cells at all.
plos-pone-0008065:
Junfeng Ji and colleagues compared the same master factors in normal and cancer stem cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. Both cell kinds can renew themselves and use the same set of pluripotency factors to do it. The puzzle is why one kind builds healthy tissue and the other builds tumors.

Side-by-side tests showed the factors do unlike jobs in the two settings. A factor that guards healthy renewal may drive growth run wild once the cell is transformed. That split gives drug hunters a hope: hit the cancer use of a factor while sparing its healthy use.
plos-pone-0008165:
Maria D'Orsogna and Tom Chou modeled the best route a virus can take through a host cell in PLOS ONE in 2009. To infect, many viruses must cross the crowded cytoplasm and pass into the nucleus. Along the way their cargo is unpacked and rebuilt into a form fit to enter.

The model weighs speed against that rebuilding: rush, and the cargo arrives unready; linger, and it may be destroyed. An optimal pace sits between. The physics sets bounds every invading virus must obey, and it may show where a drug can tip the balance against the virus.
plos-pone-0008265:
Janet E. Foley and colleagues studied a tick-borne bacterium in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Anaplasma phagocytophilum infects humans and other animals through tick bites. It must live inside host cells to survive. During infection, hosts gain temporary resistance as immunity targets specific antigens. The bacterium varies those antigens to stay ahead.

The team traced that diversity to pseudogenes, broken gene copies held in reserve. Only selected copies are represented, and they cluster in space. Recombining these copies creates fresh antigen variants. Understanding this trick could help design vaccines against the disease it causes, granulocytic anaplasmosis.
plos-pone-0008365:
Jérôme Grimplet and colleagues built a grapevine data network in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Genomic data for grapevine grew exponentially over the previous five years. The Vitis vinifera genome had been sequenced, and transcript, protein, and metabolite data kept coming. The next critical challenge was to provide tools that integrate these layers. Separate data sets alone cannot show how a vine works.

VitisNet integrates omics data through grapevine molecular networks. Networks connect genes to the traits they jointly produce. Wine and grape breeders can use such maps to target quality traits. The resource supports systems-level grape research.
plos-pone-0008465:
Francisco de Castro and co-authors write on reverse evolution in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Some species lose the power to make food from sunlight. That loss has happened many times in the history of life. In fact, loss has occurred more often than gain. Gains gave rise to large groups of algae and plants. Losses came later, as some lines took up other ways to feed.

The paper asks what forces drive such loss. When a trait no longer pays, mutations that break it may spread. The authors weigh drift, selection, and life in new niches. Their account helps explain why a useful trait can vanish.
plos-pone-0008565:
Enn-Ling Chen and co-authors characterize water behavior in MRI in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Contrast in clinical MRI often rests on tissue water proton relaxation. Different tissues relax at different rates, creating image contrast. Yet many aspects of relaxation in complex media are not well understood. Protein solutions and real tissue are such complex media. Limited tools have hampered study of these effects. The team focus on a measure called T1rho dispersion.

They characterize how T1rho varies in protein solutions and tissue. That variation reveals interactions between water and large molecules. Better understanding could improve MRI contrast for disease detection. The paper advances the physics behind a routine clinical tool.
plos-pone-0008665:
Joseph Andrews and co-authors refine a breast cancer signature in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. They had found wide DNA methylation changes in a cell model of cancer spread. Methylation is a mark that can silence genes. Those changes came with shifts in chromosome structure. The team now combine tests across several platforms. They merge marks with gene activity and gene copy number in the same cells.

The combined view sharpens the signature of breast cancer spread. Genes both marked and misexpressed become strong candidates. Such a signature may predict which tumors will spread. It also names targets that drugs might block to stop spread.
plos-pone-0008765:
Silvio Notari, Francisco Moleres, Stephen Hunter, and colleagues examined a rare U.S. case of variant CJD. Their report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variant CJD is the human prion disease linked to tainted beef. Most cases occurred in the United Kingdom. Only a few cases were found in the United States. Where the abnormal prion protein hides in the body matters for safety.

Tests found protease-resistant prion protein across many organs. The spread went beyond the brain and tonsils. Such maps inform blood and tissue safety rules. They also show how a foodborne prion can seed the whole body.
plos-pone-0008865:
Manuela Fumagalli, Maurizio Vergari, Patrizio Pasqualetti, and colleagues asked whether the brain handles hard trade-offs differently in men and women. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Utilitarian choices weigh total gain, even when someone gets hurt. Such choices arise in medicine, war, and daily business. The brain circuits behind them were largely unknown. Gender might shape both the choices and the circuits.

Brain stimulation and scanning probed how utilitarian behavior switches on. Results differed between men and women in telling ways. A brain-level account helps explain everyday moral disagreements. The work feeds the young field of moral neuroscience.
plos-pone-0008965:
Gerald Baldridge and co-authors made tick-borne bacteria glow on command, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rickettsia bacteria live only inside other cells and ride blood-feeding arthropods. Some kinds cause typhus and spotted fevers in people. Working with them is hard because they are tricky to change in the lab.

The team rewired Rickettsia montanensis to make a green glowing protein, GFP. They put the glow gene under the bacterium's own ompB switch. When the switch is on, the bacteria light up and can be followed under a microscope. The glow tag gives researchers a new handle on these hard-to-study germs.
plos-pone-0009065:
Charles Kim and co-authors compared heart-risk protein levels across people in a Mayo Clinic study, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cardiovascular disease strikes men and women at different rates. Risk also varies between ethnic groups beyond the usual explanations. The team measured 47 newer protein markers of heart disease.

The study covered 2,561 adults, men and women of varied backgrounds. Many markers sat at different levels by sex or by ethnicity. Such gaps might explain part of the unequal disease burden. Risk scores built on one group's averages could mislead for another.
plos-pone-0009165:
Susu Zughaier and co-authors reworked a cough remedy's chemistry into inflammation fighters, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Noscapine is a plant compound sold over the counter for coughs. It is non-toxic and binds tubulin, the protein scaffolding inside cells. Its shape resembles colchicine, a tubulin drug used against inflammation.

The team tested noscapine and new brominated forms made in the lab. The new forms curbed the cell scaffolding and fought inflammation strongly. A safe old drug's family may yield brand-new medicines this way. The new forms are candidates for diseases driven by runaway inflammation.
plos-pone-0009265:
Venkatesan Radhika and co-authors published this plant study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flowers pay pollinating insects in nectar, and most crops depend on that trade. Yet the body signals that control nectar release were little known. Jasmonates, plant hormones famous for aging and defense effects, were the team's suspects.

They tested how jasmonates affect nectar secretion in flowers. These hormones also steer flower development and opening, so a nectar role would fit. Finding the hormone link explains how a plant times its reward to pollinator visits. The knowledge could matter for crops whose yields hinge on insect pollination.
plos-pone-0009365:
Ali Arbab and co-authors published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. After radiation therapy for a brain tumor, scans often cannot tell returning tumor from radiation damage. Both look alike on CT, MRI, and even PET scans. That uncertainty can stall the next treatment decision.

The team labeled killer T cells with magnetic particles, made outside the body. In rats, the labeled cells were tracked by MRI to the injury site. Tumor-seeking immune cells could, in principle, light up real cancer and spare scar tissue. The study tests that approach for separating glioma from radiation injury.
plos-pone-0009465:
Justin Boyer, Kunal Bhanot, and Rashmi Kothary examined the hearts of special mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice lack dystonin, a huge protein that links parts of a cell's inner frame. Without it, their skeletal muscles waste, a condition named dystonia musculorum. Earlier work had focused on those muscles, not on the heart.

Under the microscope, the hearts looked normal in shape and tissue. Yet tests found signs that the hearts were under stress. So a normal look can hide real strain. The result warns that this protein loss may threaten the heart too, a point that matters for like diseases in people.
plos-pone-0009565:
Guy Katriel and Lewi Stone modeled what happens when shared immunity fails in PLOS ONE in 2010. When enough people are immune to a disease, even the unprotected gain some shelter. That effect is called herd immunity. It can break down if immunity falls or the germ changes. The team built a mathematical model of pandemic spread under those conditions.

The model finds the points at which the shared shield gives way. Past those points, outbreaks can grow fast among the unprotected. Work of this kind helps planners see the stakes of vaccination coverage. It shows why keeping immunity high protects everyone, not just those who are immune.
plos-pone-0009665:
Amandine Chatagnon and co-authors studied hormone response fine tuning in PLOS ONE in 2010. Estrogen switches many genes on or off in breast and other tissues. One estrogen responsive gene is pS2, also called TFF1. The team examined a protein called MBD2, which reads chemical tags on DNA. They asked how MBD2 modulates the gene's response to estrogen.

MBD2 altered the strength and timing of the response at that gene. Such modulation helps explain why hormone signals differ between cells and patients. The detail matters for breast cancer, where estrogen drives growth and drugs block its action. Fine tuners like MBD2 may shape who responds to those drugs.
plos-pone-0009865:
Many biological models pulse in cycles, from heartbeats to daily rhythms. Mochamad Apri and colleagues offered a faster way to judge how robust such models are. Their method appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

A robustness region is the range of settings where a model still behaves well. Oscillatory behavior means the model swings back and forth in a steady pattern. Estimating that region efficiently saves heavy computing time. Biological models are math versions of living processes. Modelers can then trust their models across wider conditions. Oscillations drive much of biology, from sleep to cell cycles.
plos-pone-0009965:
Measuring a fast chemical change inside cells usually takes slow, fussy lab work. Hector Aguilar and colleagues sped that measurement up with a high-throughput assay. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myosin is the motor protein that powers muscle movement.

The change is phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain, a switch for muscle contraction. In-cell Western assays read the signal inside intact cells, in bulk. The authors compared the new assays with classic Western immunoblots. Faster quantification helps labs screen many samples at once. High-throughput means testing many samples in parallel.
plos-pone-0010065:
Janet Higgins, Paul Bailey, and David Laurie compared flowering genes across grasses in 2010. Their PLOS ONE study used Brachypodium distachyon as the model plant. That small grass stands in for temperate cereals such as barley, wheat, and oats. Flowering time decides when those crops set seed, so its control genes matter to farming.

The authors compared Brachypodium genes with those of rice and the model plant Arabidopsis. Shared and divergent pathways show which flowering controls are old and which are grass-specific. Such maps help breeders tune flowering to local seasons and a changing climate.
plos-pone-0010165:
Steve Bellan reconsidered a basic assumption in disease models in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Most models of mosquito-borne disease assume mosquitoes die at a constant rate. New field research, though, suggests death rates often depend on mosquito age. That difference can change how diseases like malaria spread and how control measures perform.

Bellan built a simple model that lets mosquito mortality vary with age. He also weighed the extrinsic incubation period, the time a parasite needs inside the mosquito. More realistic survival curves can shift which control strategies look best on paper.
plos-pone-0010265:
The authors were Ana Ferreira, Rodrigo Ferreira, Dimple Rajgor, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study watched doctors reason through real cases. Little was known about how physicians actually make decisions in practice. Diagnostic guidelines assume a tidier logic than real clinics allow, so the team recorded reasoning in a real life environment.

From transcripts of that reasoning, they argue real clinical thinking runs on bounded rationality. Doctors use good-enough shortcuts under time and information limits. Guidelines that ignore those limits, they suggest, will keep missing how diagnosis really happens at the bedside.
plos-pone-0010365:
Abhik Bandyopadhyay and colleagues combined two cancer drugs in mouse breast tumors for PLOS ONE in 2010. A change in tumor cells, called EMT, can make cancers spread and resist drugs. A signal protein named TGF-beta strongly drives that change. The team paired a standard drug, doxorubicin, with a small compound that blocks TGF-beta. They tested the pair in mouse models of metastatic breast cancer.

Blocking the signal aimed to stop tumor cells from gaining stem-like traits. Those traits are tied to relapse after treatment. The drug pair thus attacks both the tumor bulk and its hardest cells. Mouse success is only a first step toward human use. Still, the logic of pairing a killer drug with an anti-spread drug is clearly laid out.
plos-pone-0010465:
Andrey Alexeyenko and colleagues mapped gene networks in zebrafish poisoned by dioxin for PLOS ONE in 2010. Dioxin is a potent pollutant that harms developing animals. How it causes its damage, step by step, is still being pieced together. The team exposed developing zebrafish embryos to dioxin. They then read changes across all genes and placed them in a changing network context.

Networks show which genes act as hubs when poison strikes. Hubs are promising places to explain the whole toxic response. Zebrafish embryos are transparent and grow fast, making them ideal for such work. The approach turns a flat gene list into a mechanism sketch. It may apply to many other poisons whose pathways are murky.
plos-pone-0010565:
Ryan Chao and colleagues studied a boy born with one very small eye. Their report, in PLOS ONE in 2010, led to a gene for eye development. Missing or tiny eyes at birth are serious defects whose causes are partly unknown. The patient had severe one-sided microphthalmia. Testing found a deleted stretch of chromosome, inherited from his mother, who was unaffected. Within that stretch lay the gene TMX3.

Further work supported TMX3 as important for building the eye. A single patient's deletion can thus expose a developmental gene. Such finds help counsel families and guide screening of similar cases. They also add pieces to the puzzle of how eyes form. The study is a clear case of bedside observation driving gene discovery.
plos-pone-0010665:
Erin Spicer and colleagues studied adhesion control in frog embryos, in PLOS ONE in 2010. During gastrulation, frog cells fold inward to form the body layers. Cells grip their matrix through anchors called integrins, and the grip must tighten and loosen on cue.

A protein named kermit2 binds the main integrin used at this stage. It pulls the integrin inside the cell, removing it from the surface. That removal times the grip changes the folding tissue needs. The work shows how embryos steer shape change by recycling anchors, not just by building new ones.
plos-pone-0010765:
Yaroslav Nikolaev and colleagues found that parts of two gene-switch proteins can also cut RNA, in PLOS ONE in 2010. GCN4 and c-Jun belong to the bZIP family, proteins that pair up through a zipper-like segment and bind DNA. Zippers are workhorses of protein design because they pair so reliably.

Isolated zipper segments showed ribonuclease activity: they broke RNA chains. No one had assigned that job to a DNA-binding segment before. Moonlighting parts blur the tidy one-protein-one-job chart. They also hint that some RNA cutting blamed on other enzymes may start with these familiar proteins, a claim other labs can now test.
plos-pone-0010865:
Xin Huang, Anke van den Berg, Zifen Gao and co-authors published this lymphoma study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma is a cancer of the lymph system, and its tumor cells often hide from the immune system by dropping the HLA molecules that display cell contents. Work in European patients tied HLA display to infection with Epstein-Barr virus, so the team checked Chinese patients.

They examined tumor samples from five hospitals in northern China, classifying each case and testing for the virus. About two-fifths of the tumors carried Epstein-Barr virus. The group then measured HLA class I and class II display on the tumor cells to compare virus-positive and virus-negative cases. Huang and colleagues extend a mostly European research line to a new population, where patterns of immune escape may not match.
plos-pone-0010965:
Ashleigh Boyd and Kathryn Wood published this transplantation study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stem cells can be grown into insulin-producing clusters that might one day treat diabetes, but the immune system's first responders may attack such grafts before any lasting response develops. The authors measured that early innate reaction in mice receiving these lab-grown clusters.

Neutrophils and macrophages moved into the transplant site immediately, yet the infiltration faded by the third day. Gene profiling found inflammatory signals absent or sharply reduced by then, and the reaction was milder than the one provoked by transplanting natural pancreatic islets. Boyd and Wood suggest lab-grown insulin cells start with an immunological advantage. Knowing the early response window helps design the protective steps a future cell therapy would need.
plos-pone-0011065:
Gudrun Weiss, Simon Rasmussen, Lisbeth Nielsen Fink and co-authors published this probiotic study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two familiar gut bacteria affect the immune system's teaching cells in opposite ways. Lactobacillus acidophilus provokes a strong inflammatory, antiviral-style response. Bifidobacteria stay quiet. They even block the first bacterium's effect. The authors used genome-wide arrays to see the full conversation.

Mouse teaching cells exposed to the first bacterium switched on interferon-beta and virus defense genes. They also raised a broad set of signaling genes. The second bacterium instead raised a different, innate-focused set. When both were present, it actively rewrote the profile the first one induced. Weiss and colleagues show these strains are not interchangeable: one species can edit another's immune message. That matters for designing health foods with predictable effects.
plos-pone-0011165:
A trial team in Zambia tested infant nutrition in a 2010 PLOS ONE report, with authors not named in the record. Babies received food enriched with vitamins and minerals. The trial included infants whose mothers had HIV and infants whose mothers did not, and tracked growth and health in both groups.

Enriched food aimed to fill nutrient gaps during a critical window of early growth. Such gaps can stunt growth and weaken health for years. A randomized trial gives strong evidence for or against the approach. Its results can guide child health programs in Zambia and similar settings on whether enrichment is worth its cost.
plos-pone-0011265:
Shah, Sunderland and Grdzelishvili tested an antiviral drug in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ribavirin is used against several viruses, yet it works better in some settings than others. The team measured resistance of two model viruses to the drug across different cell types used in labs.

Resistance depended on which cell type hosted the virus, not on the virus alone. That nuance can mislead drug testing if only one cell line is used. It also matters for dosing, since body tissues differ like lab cells do. Knowing the host effect could rescue therapies judged as failures too early.
plos-pone-0011365:
K Viswanath and colleagues used a national survey in 2010 to test whether screens shape tobacco use in India. India carries a heavy tobacco burden, and films and television there reach huge audiences, often showing smoking as glamorous or normal. The team asked whether people more exposed to such media were more likely to use tobacco themselves.

Drawing on survey data from across the country, they found a clear link between screen exposure and tobacco use. The pattern held as a population-level signal, not just an anecdote about a few viewers. The result gives health officials in India evidence for tighter rules on smoking in films and shows. It also supports media campaigns that counter the image of tobacco that entertainment so often sells.
plos-pone-0011465:
Matthew Peirce and co-authors identified in 2010 a scaffold protein that selectively tunes alarm signaling in macrophages. Macrophages spot germs through Toll-like receptors and answer by releasing cytokine alarms. Many proteins pass that signal along, but scaffold proteins decide its strength and flavor by holding the relay team together. The team characterized one such scaffold, Themis2, also called ICB1.

The scaffold regulated macrophage Toll-like receptor signaling in a selective way, affecting some cytokine outputs more than others. A selective knob is more useful than a master switch, since it might calm harmful inflammation without silencing defense entirely. The finding adds a control point on the immune front line. For diseases of runaway inflammation, selective tuning of this kind is exactly what safer drugs will need.
plos-pone-0011565:
Michael Wilson and co-authors tested in 2010 the paradox of carbon monoxide as a lung treatment. The gas is famous as a silent killer in faulty heaters, yet the body makes tiny amounts of it naturally, and small doses calm inflammation in animal studies. The team gave inhaled carbon monoxide to mice with pulmonary inflammation and measured both benefit and safety in the same experiment.

A therapy that is poison at one dose and medicine at another lives or dies on its margin, so testing efficacy and safety together is the honest design. Their results inform whether the gas can soothe injured lungs without harming the animal that breathes it. Inhaled delivery is attractive because the lung, the target, receives the dose first.
